docs.title: Welcome To The Guide To FRC Java
docs.text:
This site serves as a starting point for learning to code for FRC.

Make your way through the pages to gain a foundation for programming on the team.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: If you're new, start with the Getting Started Guide to set up your tools and environment.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Java Basics: the Java you need, with code you can run and edit right on the page.
  • FRC-Specific Programming: how a robot program runs and the Java that shows up in every project.
    • Subsystems: a mechanism split into IO classes and a state machine.
    • RobotContainer: building the robot and connecting the controller.
    • RobotState: the robot's brain, turning one button into the right state for every subsystem.
    • Constants: where every number lives, and how to tune it while the robot runs.

Most pages have live editors and practice challenges. You don't need to install anything to try them. The robot examples run in a pretend WPILib that lives in your browser.

docs.title: Interactive Code Editors
docs.text: Two kinds of fenced blocks turn into live widgets. Both are plain Markdown, so there is nothing to build or install. The code that runs them lives in docs/javascripts/ (minijava.js is a small Java interpreter, wpilib-prelude.js is a pretend WPILib, and playground.js makes the widgets).

docs.title: Playground
docs.text:
A playground block is an editable Java program with a Run button. Lines starting with //@ set options and must come before the code.

```playground
//@ title: Change a member
//@ goal: Press Run, then change the message.
String message = "hello world";
System.out.println(message);
```

To make it a graded challenge, add a hidden test below the starter code. The student's code is checked when they press Check my code.

```playground
//@ title: Write a method
//@ goal: Write a method named doubleIt that returns number * 2.
//@ require: int\s+doubleIt\s*\( | Name the method doubleIt and return an int.
// Write your method here:

//@@ harness
System.out.println(doubleIt(4));
//@@ expect
8
//@@ hint
The header looks like `public int doubleIt(int number)`.
//@@ solution
public int doubleIt(int number) {
    return number * 2;
}
//@@ explain
Shown after the student passes.
```
Line Meaning //@ title: / //@ goal: Heading and instructions above the editor //@ require: regex \| message The code must match the pattern, otherwise the message is shown //@ mode: predict Student predicts the output instead of writing code //@ prelude: wpilib Loads the pretend WPILib (no import needed) //@ panel: robot Shows the robot simulator and virtual controller. It starts a class named Robot (or RobotContainer if there is no Robot) //@ show: controller,motors,dashboard,scheduler Which parts of the simulator panel to display (default is all four) //@ dio: 0,1 Adds a toggle button for each digital input channel, for pretend limit switches and sensors //@@ harness Hidden code appended when checking //@@ expect Exact output the check must produce //@@ hint Repeatable. docs.title: Checking your work
docs.text:
Broken exercises are easy to write by accident, such as a solution that doesn't pass its own test. Before opening a pull request, run:

node tools/check-lessons.js

It runs every playground and quiz on the site and checks that each starter fails, each solution passes, and every quiz question has a correct answer. node tools/test-minijava.js and node tools/test-wpilib.js test the interpreter and the pretend WPILib. CI runs all three before deploying.

Students' progress

Progress is saved in each student's own browser, so it stays on their device and can be cleared by them.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Welcome! Your journey as a programmer for FRC starts here. Before we being programming, there are a few things we must download and get set up.

docs.title: Installing WPILib VS Code
docs.text:
WPILib is an open-source framework for FRC programming provided by the WPI Institute. They provide WPILib VS Code, which is what we will be using to code.

Go here and scroll down to download the installer. This should download an iso file.

Once you finish downloading, double click the .iso file to open it in your file explorer. Here, double click WPILibInstaller.exe.

If you get a "Windows protected your PC" prompt, hit "More info" then "Run anyway". This should show once you hit start:

Select the options from above and hit install for this user. Next, select Download for this computer only.

Once it finishes installing, you can close the window. WPILib is now installed.

docs.title: Installing Git
docs.text:
422, and most organizations around the world use Github to store their code. Similar to Google Docs, Github is a repository where code it stored so that everyone can access it. Git is a command line tool that will allow us to pull the code from the online Github repository onto our own machine so that we can edit the code.

WindowsMacBooks

Go here and download the Git for Windows/x64 Setup option.

Open the installer and hit next until you get to the install button. Hit install.

Once done, uncheck both boxes and hit finish.

MacBooks

Most MacBooks today ship with Git already installed. If you are unsure if you have it, skip this step and move to testing Git to check it out.

MacBooks without Git already installed will need to install Homebrew first. Open your terminal and paste the following line into it and hit enter: 

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
Once you finish installing Homebrew, paste the following line into the temrinal and hit enter: 
brew install git

docs.title: Testing WPILib and Git
docs.text:
This is the final step. Once you have both WPILib and Git installed, you can test Git.

Open WPILib VS Code. On Windows, this comes in the search window as VS Code, not VSCode. Once you open it, you should be presented with something similar to this screen:

Hit Ctrl+Shift+~ to enter the terminal (CMD+Shift+~ on MacBooks). Type the following and hit enter to check if git is working: 

git --version
If you get something similar to below, Git is working. 
git version 2.51.0.windows.1

Finished

If you have successfully installed WPILib and Git and ensured Git is working, you are set to code for 422!

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
A robot is full of numbers: CAN ids, gear ratios, how far the climber can swing, how hard the elevator motor should push, how close is "close enough." If those numbers are scattered through twenty files, changing one means hunting for it, and changing it in one place but not another gives you a robot that disagrees with itself.

So we put them all in one file, Constants.java. On our 2025 robot it's about 900 lines, and it's the file you'll open the most while tuning.

docs.title: One class per mechanism
docs.text:
Constants doesn't hold a giant list of numbers. It holds a set of nested classes, one per mechanism, so the climber's numbers sit together and don't get mixed up with the elevator's.

Constants.java, shortened
public final class Constants {
    public static final class ClimbConstants {
        public static final double kClimbTolerance = 5.0; // degrees

        public static final double kClimbReduction = (5.0 / 1.0) * (4.0 / 1.0) * (68.0 / 18.0);

        public static final Rotation2d kMinAngle = Rotation2d.fromDegrees(-350.0);
        public static final Rotation2d kMaxAngle = Rotation2d.fromDegrees(600.0);
    }

    public static final class ElevatorConstants {
        // ...
    }

    public static final class Ports {
        public static final int kClimbMotor = 36;
        public static final String kDriveCanivoreName = "Drivetrain"; // the CAN bus's name
        // ...
    }
}

Everything here is the static final combination from FRC Nuances: static so you can use it without creating an object, and final so nothing can change it while the robot runs. A few habits to notice:

  • Names start with k and are in camel case: kClimbTolerance. (This is a WPILib habit. The k means "constant".)
  • Units go in a comment whenever there are any: // degrees, // meters per second. A bare 5.0 could mean anything. There's a spot in our code where a comment says "these are magic units", and that's a warning, not an example.
  • Write gear ratios as the stages they are. (5.0 / 1.0) * (4.0 / 1.0) * (68.0 / 18.0) looks silly next to 75.56, but it's the one you can check against the gearbox on the robot.

To use one, you reach in through the outer class, or import the inner class so you can drop the prefix:

double tolerance = Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbTolerance;

// or, with  import frc.robot.Constants.ClimbConstants;  at the top of the file:
double tolerance = ClimbConstants.kClimbTolerance;

Your turn. Write the nested class so Climb can use it.

//@ title: Write a constants class
//@ goal: Inside Constants, write a public static final class ClimbConstants with three doubles: kClimbTolerance = 5.0, kClimbStowPos = -225.0 and kClimbDeployPos = 600.0.
//@ lines: 20
//@ require: static\s+final\s+class\s+ClimbConstants | Write a public static final class named ClimbConstants inside Constants.
//@ require: double\s+kClimbTolerance | Add kClimbTolerance as a double.
public class Constants {
    // Write ClimbConstants here:

}

public class Climb {
    public boolean atSetpoint(double desiredDegrees, double currentDegrees) {
        return Math.abs(desiredDegrees - currentDegrees) < Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbTolerance;
    }
}
//@@ harness
Climb climb = new Climb();
System.out.println(climb.atSetpoint(600.0, 597.0));
System.out.println(climb.atSetpoint(600.0, 590.0));
System.out.println(Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbStowPos);
System.out.println(Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbDeployPos);
//@@ expect
true
false
-225.0
600.0
//@@ hint
The class goes inside `Constants`, between its curly braces: `public static final class ClimbConstants { ... }`.
//@@ hint
Each constant looks like `public static final double kClimbTolerance = 5.0; // degrees`.
//@@ solution
public class Constants {
    public static final class ClimbConstants {
        public static final double kClimbTolerance = 5.0; // degrees
        public static final double kClimbStowPos = -225.0; // degrees
        public static final double kClimbDeployPos = 600.0; // degrees
    }
}

public class Climb {
    public boolean atSetpoint(double desiredDegrees, double currentDegrees) {
        return Math.abs(desiredDegrees - currentDegrees) < Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbTolerance;
    }
}
//@@ explain
Now the tolerance has one home. If the climber needs to be more precise, you change one number, and everything that uses `kClimbTolerance` follows.

docs.title: Numbers you tune on the robot
docs.text:
Some numbers you can't know ahead of time. How hard should the climber's PID push? How high should the elevator go to score? You find out by trying a value, watching the robot, and adjusting. If every change meant editing code, building, and deploying (a minute or more each time), tuning would take all day.

So our tuning numbers aren't plain doubles. They're LoggedTunableNumbers.

Constants.java
public static final class ClimbConstants {
    public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbP = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb P", 30.0);
    public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbI = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb I", 0.0);
    public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbD = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb D", 0.0);

    public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbStowPos =
        new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb Stow Angle", -225.0);
}

A LoggedTunableNumber has a name, which is how it shows up on the dashboard, and a default, the number in the code. While the robot runs in tuning mode, you can change it from the dashboard and the robot picks up the new value right away, no deploy needed.

Because it's an object and not a double, you read it with .get():

m_io.setDesiredAngle(Rotation2d.fromDegrees(ClimbConstants.kClimbStowPos.get()), 0.0);

Always call .get() where you use the number, instead of saving it into a variable once. A saved copy never notices that you changed it.

Here is the idea in miniature. This pretend arm moves a fraction (kP) of the remaining distance toward 100 each loop. Run it, then change kP and run it again. Try 0.05, 0.5, and 1.5. A value that's too small is slow, and one that's too big overshoots and swings back and forth.

//@ title: Tune it
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: Change kP's default and press Run each time. Try 0.05, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5. Which one gets to 100 fastest without overshooting?
//@ lines: 14
LoggedTunableNumber kP = new LoggedTunableNumber("Arm P", 0.2);

double position = 0.0;
double target = 100.0;

for (int loop = 1; loop <= 10; loop++) {
    // each loop, move kP of the way to the target
    position += kP.get() * (target - position);
    System.out.println("loop " + loop + ": " + Math.round(position));
}

Tuning mode

Constants has a flag, kTuningMode. When it's true, a LoggedTunableNumber reads the dashboard. When it's false, it just returns the default from the code and nothing on the dashboard can change it. Once you find a good value on the dashboard, copy it into the code as the new default. The dashboard doesn't write your code for you.

docs.title: Only re-send when a number changes
docs.text:
There's one catch. A PID controller lives inside the motor controller, so after you change kP, the new value has to be sent to the motor over the CAN bus. You don't want to do that every 20 ms. It's traffic the bus doesn't need when nothing has changed.

LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged solves it. You give it the numbers to watch and some code to run, and it runs the code only if one of the numbers is different from last time it checked (and once at the very start).

Climb.periodic(), simplified
LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged(
    hashCode(),
    () -> m_io.setPID(0, ClimbConstants.kClimbP.get(), ClimbConstants.kClimbI.get(), ClimbConstants.kClimbD.get()),
    ClimbConstants.kClimbP,
    ClimbConstants.kClimbI,
    ClimbConstants.kClimbD);

The first argument is an id, so that more than one object can watch the same number without disturbing each other. We pass hashCode(), a number that's different for each object. The second is the code to run, as a lambda. The rest are the numbers to watch.

Your turn. periodic() runs every loop. Make it re-send the PID to the motor only when a number changes.

//@ title: Re-send only on change
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: In periodic(), use LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged so the PID is sent to the IO only when kClimbP, kClimbI or kClimbD changes. (Without it, it would be sent every loop.)
//@ lines: 38
//@ require: ifChanged\( | Use LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged.
public class Constants {
    public static final class ClimbConstants {
        public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbP = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb P", 30.0);
        public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbI = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb I", 0.0);
        public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbD = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb D", 0.0);
    }
}

public interface ClimbIO {
    public void setPID(double kP, double kI, double kD);
}

public class ClimbIOSim implements ClimbIO {
    @Override
    public void setPID(double kP, double kI, double kD) {
        System.out.println("PID " + kP + " " + kI + " " + kD);
    }
}

public class Climb {
    private final ClimbIO m_io;

    public Climb(ClimbIO io) {
        m_io = io;
    }

    public void periodic() {
        // Send the PID to m_io only when one of the three numbers changed:

    }
}
//@@ harness
Climb climb = new Climb(new ClimbIOSim());
climb.periodic();
climb.periodic();
climb.periodic();
Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbP.set(35.0);
climb.periodic();
climb.periodic();
//@@ expect
PID 30.0 0.0 0.0
PID 35.0 0.0 0.0
//@@ hint
The call has three parts: an id (use `hashCode()`), a lambda that calls `m_io.setPID(...)`, and then the numbers to watch, separated by commas.
//@@ hint
`LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged(hashCode(), () -> m_io.setPID(kP.get(), kI.get(), kD.get()), kP, kI, kD);` where each `kP`, `kI` and `kD` is written as `Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbP` and so on.
//@@ solution
public class Constants {
    public static final class ClimbConstants {
        public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbP = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb P", 30.0);
        public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbI = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb I", 0.0);
        public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbD = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb D", 0.0);
    }
}

public interface ClimbIO {
    public void setPID(double kP, double kI, double kD);
}

public class ClimbIOSim implements ClimbIO {
    @Override
    public void setPID(double kP, double kI, double kD) {
        System.out.println("PID " + kP + " " + kI + " " + kD);
    }
}

public class Climb {
    private final ClimbIO m_io;

    public Climb(ClimbIO io) {
        m_io = io;
    }

    public void periodic() {
        LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged(
            hashCode(),
            () -> m_io.setPID(
                Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbP.get(),
                Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbI.get(),
                Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbD.get()),
            Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbP,
            Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbI,
            Constants.ClimbConstants.kClimbD);
    }
}
//@@ explain
Five loops ran, but the PID was only sent twice: once at the start, and once after the number changed. The harness's `set(35.0)` plays the part of you typing a new value into the dashboard.

docs.title: Real and simulated numbers
docs.text:
A simulated motor isn't a real motor. It has no friction, no battery sag, and no gearbox slop, so the gains that work on the real climber might make the simulated one swing wildly. So ClimbConstants has a second set of numbers just for simulation.

ClimbConstants (shortened)
// real: tunable from the dashboard
public static final LoggedTunableNumber kClimbP = new LoggedTunableNumber("Climb P", 30.0);

// sim constants
public static final double kSimGearing = 1.0;
public static final DCMotor kSimGearbox = DCMotor.getKrakenX60(1);
public static final double kSimClimbArmLengthMeters = 0.25;
public static final double kSimClimbP = 0.5;
public static final double kSimClimbD = 0.35;

The Climb subsystem picks between them using RobotBase.isReal(), which is true on a roboRIO and false on a laptop.

Climb.java
if (RobotBase.isReal()) {
    m_io.setPID(m_currSlot, ClimbConstants.kClimbP.get(), ClimbConstants.kClimbI.get(), ClimbConstants.kClimbD.get());
} else {
    m_io.setPID(m_currSlot, ClimbConstants.kSimClimbP, ClimbConstants.kSimClimbI, ClimbConstants.kSimClimbD);
}

This is one of the few places where a subsystem checks whether it's real. Choosing which IO class to use is still the job of RobotContainer, as you saw on that page. But the numbers that make the sim behave belong to the sim, so they're picked here.

docs.title: The other constants
docs.text:
Most of the file is nested classes for mechanisms, but a few are worth knowing about:

  • Ports holds every CAN id and the name of the CAN bus: Ports.kIntakeRoller, Ports.kDriveCanivoreName. When a wire is moved, the id changes in exactly one place.
  • CurrentLimitConstants holds how much current each motor is allowed to draw. These protect the motors and the battery.
  • Robot-wide settings sit at the very top of the file.
Constants.java, the top
public static final boolean kTuningMode = true;

public static final Mode kRealMode = Mode.REAL;
public static final Mode kSimMode = Mode.SIM;
public static final Mode kCurrentMode = RobotBase.isReal() ? kRealMode : kSimMode;

// set to false to disable alerts
public static final boolean kUseAlerts = true && kCurrentMode != Mode.SIM;

kCurrentMode is the one RobotContainer switches on. kUseAlerts turns the "motor disconnected" dashboard alerts on and off. A flag here changes behavior across the whole robot, which is why it deserves a comment and a single home.

@ title: Constants
? Why does each mechanism get its own nested class, like `ClimbConstants`?
- Java requires one class per mechanism
+ So each mechanism's numbers are grouped together and don't get mixed up with the others
- It makes the numbers faster to read
- So they can be changed while the robot runs
> Grouping makes `Constants.java` easy to scan, and `ClimbConstants.kClimbTolerance` reads like what it is.

? What does the `k` at the start of `kClimbTolerance` mean?
- It's short for "kilo"
+ It marks a constant, by WPILib convention
- It means the number is tunable
- It means the number is in kilometers
> It's a naming habit. It tells you at a glance that a name is a constant, not a variable.

? You have `LoggedTunableNumber kClimbP`. How do you get its value?
- `kClimbP`
+ `kClimbP.get()`
- `kClimbP.value`
- `(double) kClimbP`
> It's an object, so you ask it for its value. Call `.get()` each time you use it so you always see the latest value.

? Why use `LoggedTunableNumber.ifChanged` instead of sending the PID every loop?
- It's required by the motor controller
+ The PID only needs to reach the motor controller when a value has changed, and sending it every loop wastes CAN bus traffic
- It makes the PID more accurate
- It saves the numbers to the log
> It runs your code once at the start, and then only after a watched number changes.

? You find the perfect P value by typing it into the dashboard. What should you do next?
- Nothing. It's saved forever.
+ Copy it into the code as the new default, so it's the value next time the robot starts
- Delete the `LoggedTunableNumber`
- Restart the dashboard
> The dashboard value isn't part of your code. The default in `Constants.java` is what the robot starts with.

? Why does `ClimbConstants` have separate `kSimClimbP` and `kClimbP` values?
- The sim is faster
+ A simulated climber behaves differently from the real one, so it needs its own gains
- Because `kClimbP` can't be used in simulation
- To save memory
> The numbers that make a pretend motor behave well don't match the numbers for a real one.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: That's the whole structure of our robot code, from a button press all the way to a motor: a binding asks RobotState for an action, which sets each subsystem's state, which runs through an IO class using numbers from Constants. Now you know where to look in the real code. Open the FRC-25 repository and trace a button from RobotContainer down to a ClimbIOKraken.

docs.title: FRC Nuances
docs.text:
You now know enough Java to read most robot code. This page covers what is different about programming a robot, and the handful of Java features that show up in every FRC project but that a normal Java course barely touches.

Everything with a code editor on this page runs right in your browser. It isn't the real WPILib, but it is a pretend version with the same class names and the same shape, so what you write here is what you'd write on the robot.

About the simulator

The in-browser robot understands a small slice of WPILib: subsystems, commands, triggers, the scheduler, Xbox controllers, a motor controller, and DifferentialDrive. You don't need import lines in the editors on this site. Real projects do, and the sections below show them.

Our way of writing robot code

If you search for FRC tutorials, you'll find many that put commands inside every subsystem. Our team does it differently. Each mechanism is split into small, swappable layers, and the whole robot is driven by states. That structure comes from the code we actually run, and the next few pages teach it. When something here looks different from an online tutorial, this is why.

docs.title: Your code doesn't run top to bottom
docs.text:
In the Java lessons, your program ran from the first line to the last and then stopped. A robot program is different. It starts, and then WPILib calls your code over and over, 50 times every second (once every 20 milliseconds), until the robot is switched off. You don't write that loop. You write the pieces WPILib calls, and WPILib decides when.

Which pieces get called depends on what mode the robot is in, which the Driver Station controls:

Mode Runs once when it starts Runs every 20 ms Any robotInit() (at startup) robotPeriodic() Disabled disabledInit() disabledPeriodic() Autonomous autonomousInit() autonomousPeriodic() Teleop teleopInit() teleopPeriodic()

Once the robot is on, press the buttons to switch modes and watch the counter. The dashboard on the right is SmartDashboard, which is how robot code shows numbers to the drivers.

//@ title: The 20 ms loop
//@ panel: robot
//@ show: dashboard
//@ goal: Press Run, then switch the robot between disabled, auto and teleop. Only teleop makes this counter move. Try changing teleopPeriodic to autonomousPeriodic.
//@ lines: 14
public class Robot extends TimedRobot {
    private int m_ticks = 0;

    @Override
    public void teleopPeriodic() {
        m_ticks++;
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Loop count", m_ticks);
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Seconds", m_ticks / 50.0);
    }
}

Now see if you can predict the order WPILib calls things in. Read it carefully, because robotPeriodic() is easy to get wrong.

//@ title: What order do things run in?
//@ mode: predict
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: This starts the robot, switches to teleop, and runs 2 loops. Type the 6 lines it prints.
//@ lines: 18
public class Robot extends TimedRobot {
    @Override public void robotInit()      { System.out.println("robotInit"); }
    @Override public void teleopInit()     { System.out.println("teleopInit"); }
    @Override public void teleopPeriodic() { System.out.println("teleopPeriodic"); }
    @Override public void robotPeriodic()  { System.out.println("robotPeriodic"); }
}

Sim.start(new Robot());
Sim.setMode("teleop");
Sim.loops(2);
//@@ explain
The `Init` methods run once. After that, each loop calls the mode's periodic method first and `robotPeriodic()` second. Two loops means two of each pair.

Why 20 ms matters

Your periodic code has to finish well inside 20 ms. Don't put loops that wait, sleep, or take a long time in there. If your code is slow, the whole robot gets sluggish. This is also why we avoid Thread.sleep in robot code.

docs.title: The files in a robot project
docs.text:
When WPILib creates a project for you, your code lives in src/main/java/frc/robot. Here is how our team's robot code is organized.

Our project layout
src/main/java/frc/
├── robot/
│   ├── Main.java             Starts the program. Never edit this.
│   ├── Robot.java            The modes. Also sets up logging.
│   ├── RobotContainer.java   Creates every subsystem and controller, connects buttons.
│   ├── RobotState.java       The robot's "brain": what is it trying to do right now?
│   ├── Constants.java        Numbers that belong in one place: CAN IDs, speeds, tuning.
│   ├── subsystems/           One folder per mechanism.
│   │   ├── drive/
│   │   │   └── Drive.java    The drivetrain, plus IO classes for its gyro and swerve modules.
│   │   └── intake/
│   │       ├── Intake.java               The subsystem: its states and its logic.
│   │       ├── pivot/                    The arm that swings the intake out.
│   │       │   ├── PivotIO.java          The list of things the hardware can do.
│   │       │   ├── PivotIOKraken.java    Talks to the real motors.
│   │       │   ├── PivotIOSim.java       A pretend pivot for simulation.
│   │       │   └── PivotIOReplay.java    Does nothing, used when replaying a log.
│   │       └── roller/                   The wheels that grab the game piece. The same
│   │                                     four files: IntakeRollerIO, IntakeRollerIOKraken,
│   │                                     IntakeRollerIOSim, IntakeRollerIOReplay.
│   ├── oi/                   Controller classes: which button means what.
│   ├── commands/             Only drive commands and autonomous routines.
│   └── util/                 Helpers shared by everything.
└── lib/                      Code we borrowed from other teams and libraries.

graph TD
    M["Main.java<br>starts the program"] --> R["Robot.java<br>runs every 20 ms"]
    R --> RC["RobotContainer.java<br>builds everything"]
    RC --> S["Subsystems<br>own the hardware"]
    RC --> C["Controllers (oi/)<br>watch the buttons"]
    C -->|"set what the robot is doing"| RS["RobotState<br>the brain"]
    RS -->|"set each subsystem's state"| S
    S -->|"uses"| IO["IO classes<br>real, sim or replay"]

You will spend most of your time in these places:

  • Subsystems run one mechanism as a set of states, and talk to hardware only through an IO class. See Subsystems.
  • RobotContainer builds everything and connects buttons. See RobotContainer.
  • RobotState decides what the whole robot is doing, and tells each subsystem. See RobotState.
  • Constants holds every number you might need to change. See Constants.

Robot.java stays mostly as it is. Our robot extends LoggedRobot instead of the usual TimedRobot. A LoggedRobot is a TimedRobot that also records everything the robot does into a log file, which we can replay later on a laptop. The part that matters is in robotPeriodic():

Robot.java
@Override
public void robotPeriodic() {
    RobotState.getInstance().updateRobotState();
    CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
}

Every 20 ms, RobotState decides what the robot should be doing, and then the command scheduler polls the buttons, runs any active commands and calls every subsystem's periodic() method. The scheduler is still the engine that keeps everything ticking. If you delete that one line, the robot does nothing.

@ title: Which file?
? You want to change which CAN ID the intake motor uses. Where is the best place?
- `Main.java`
- `Robot.java`
+ `Constants.java`
- `RobotContainer.java`
> Numbers like CAN IDs live in `Constants.java` so you can find and change them in one place.

? You want the A button to start the intake. Where does that binding go?
- `Main.java`
- `IntakeSubsystem.java`
+ `RobotContainer.java`
- `Constants.java`
> `RobotContainer` connects controller buttons to commands.

? You want the whole robot to switch into "intaking" mode when the driver presses a button. Which file keeps track of what the robot is doing?
- `Main.java`
- `Constants.java`
+ `RobotState.java`
- `ElevatorIOSim.java`
> `RobotState` is the robot's brain. It remembers the current action and tells each subsystem what to do.

? Which class talks to the real motors on the elevator?
- `Elevator`
- `ElevatorIO`
+ `ElevatorIOKraken`
- `ElevatorIOSim`
> `ElevatorIOKraken` is the only one that touches real hardware. `Elevator` only ever talks to the `ElevatorIO` interface.

? Which file should you never edit?
+ `Main.java`
- `Robot.java`
- `Constants.java`
- `RobotContainer.java`
> WPILib handles `Main.java`. It just starts your robot.

? Which line in `robotPeriodic()` calls every subsystem's `periodic()` method?
- `SmartDashboard.updateValues();`
+ `CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();`
- `RobotContainer.run();`
- `super.periodic();`
> The scheduler polls buttons, runs commands and calls subsystem `periodic()` methods.

docs.title: Java you will see in every robot project
docs.text: These are the Java features that robot code leans on. Most of them you have partly seen already.

docs.title: package and import
docs.text:
Every file in a real project begins with a package line, which says which folder it lives in, and import lines, which tell Java where to find the classes you use. WPILib and vendor libraries each have their own.

IntakeSubsystem.java
package frc.robot.subsystems;

import com.revrobotics.spark.SparkLowLevel.MotorType;
import com.revrobotics.spark.SparkMax;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase;

You almost never type these by hand. VS Code underlines a class it can't find in red. Click it and choose the quick fix Import, or press Ctrl + . (Cmd + . on a Mac) while your cursor is on it. The editors on this site skip imports so you can focus on the code.

docs.title: extends: inheriting from a class
docs.text:
When a class extends another, it automatically gets everything the other class has. Almost everything in command-based programming is built this way. Your subsystem extends SubsystemBase, so it inherits what makes it a subsystem.

Here is the powerful part. SubsystemBase registers every subsystem with the scheduler when it's created, and the scheduler calls each one's periodic() method every loop. You never call periodic() yourself. Run it and watch.

//@ title: periodic() is called for you
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: Run it. Notice that nothing in the code calls periodic(). Then add a second subsystem called Intake that prints its own message.
//@ lines: 14
public class Arm extends SubsystemBase {
    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        System.out.println("Arm periodic");
    }
}

Arm arm = new Arm();

// This is what Robot.java does for you every 20 ms:
CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();

Now try it yourself. This class has the right method but forgot to extend anything, so the scheduler has no idea it exists.

//@ title: Make Arm a subsystem
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: Make Arm a real subsystem so the scheduler calls its periodic() method.
//@ lines: 10
//@ require: extends\s+SubsystemBase | Make Arm extend SubsystemBase.
//@ require: @Override | Mark periodic() with @Override.
public class Arm {
    public void periodic() {
        System.out.println("Arm is alive");
    }
}
//@@ harness
Arm arm = new Arm();
CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
//@@ expect
Arm is alive
Arm is alive
//@@ hint
Add `extends SubsystemBase` after the class name.
//@@ hint
Put `@Override` on its own line above `public void periodic()`. This tells Java that you are replacing a method from the parent class.
//@@ solution
public class Arm extends SubsystemBase {
    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        System.out.println("Arm is alive");
    }
}
//@@ explain
`SubsystemBase` does the registering for you. All you do is override `periodic()` with what you want to happen each loop.

docs.title: @Override
docs.text:
@Override is a promise to Java: "this method replaces one from the parent class." If you spell it wrong or give it the wrong inputs, Java stops you, instead of silently never calling it. Without @Override, a typo like periodc() is just a new method that nobody calls, and you'd spend an hour wondering why nothing happens.

//@ title: The typo that @Override catches
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: Press Run and read the error message. Fix the typo, then press Check my code.
//@ lines: 8
public class Arm extends SubsystemBase {
    @Override
    public void periodc() {
        System.out.println("Arm periodic");
    }
}
//@@ harness
Arm arm = new Arm();
CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
//@@ expect
Arm periodic
//@@ hint
Look closely at the method name. Compare it to `periodic`.
//@@ solution
public class Arm extends SubsystemBase {
    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        System.out.println("Arm periodic");
    }
}
//@@ explain
"Method does not override or implement a method from a supertype" always means one thing: the name or inputs don't match the parent's method. Always add `@Override`, and let Java catch typos for you.

docs.title: final, static, and constants
docs.text:
You'll see these everywhere, usually together.

  • final means the variable can never be reassigned after it's set. A motor controller is created once and never swapped out, so we write private final SparkMax m_motor.
  • static means the thing belongs to the class itself, not to each object. So no matter how many objects of a class you make, changing a static variable for one of them changes it for all the objects at the same time. It also means you can use it without creating an object at all, like Math.abs(x) or Constants.kMaxSpeed.
  • A static final value is a constant: one fixed number that lives in one place.

WPILib teams, including ours, follow two naming habits, and you'll see them in every project:

Convention Used for Example m_ prefix Member fields of an object m_motor, m_driverController k prefix Constants kMotorId, kIntakeSpeed

Robot constants live in Constants.java, grouped into small nested classes so related numbers stay together.

//@ title: A Constants file
//@ goal: Run it. Then change kIntakeSpeed and add a new constant of your own, like kOuttakeSpeed, and print it.
//@ lines: 18
public class Constants {
    public static final class IntakeConstants {
        public static final int kMotorId = 5;
        public static final double kIntakeSpeed = 0.8;
    }

    public static final class DriveConstants {
        public static final int kLeftMotorId = 1;
        public static final int kRightMotorId = 2;
    }
}

System.out.println("Intake motor on CAN id " + Constants.IntakeConstants.kMotorId);
System.out.println("Intake speed " + Constants.IntakeConstants.kIntakeSpeed);
System.out.println("Left drive motor on CAN id " + Constants.DriveConstants.kLeftMotorId);
//@ title: Add constants
//@ goal: Inside ArmConstants, add two constants: an int called kMotorId set to 9, and a double called kMaxSpeed set to 0.4.
//@ lines: 12
//@ require: static\s+final\s+int\s+kMotorId | Declare kMotorId as public static final int.
//@ require: static\s+final\s+double\s+kMaxSpeed | Declare kMaxSpeed as public static final double.
public class Constants {
    public static final class ArmConstants {
        // Add your constants here

    }
}
//@@ harness
System.out.println(Constants.ArmConstants.kMotorId);
System.out.println(Constants.ArmConstants.kMaxSpeed);
//@@ expect
9
0.4
//@@ hint
The pattern is `public static final type kName = value;`
//@@ solution
public class Constants {
    public static final class ArmConstants {
        public static final int kMotorId = 9;
        public static final double kMaxSpeed = 0.4;
    }
}
//@@ explain
If the arm motor ever changes CAN id, you fix it in exactly one place, and every file that uses `kMotorId` picks up the change.
@ title: final and static
? What does `private final SparkMax m_motor;` mean?
- The motor can only be used once
+ The variable `m_motor` can't be pointed at a different motor after it's set
- The motor is faster than a regular one
- The motor is shared by all robots
> `final` locks the variable so it can't be reassigned.

? How would you read a constant `kMaxSpeed` inside `Constants.DriveConstants` from another class?
- `new DriveConstants().kMaxSpeed`
+ `Constants.DriveConstants.kMaxSpeed`
- `kMaxSpeed.DriveConstants.Constants`
- `Constants(DriveConstants).kMaxSpeed`
> Static members belong to the class, so you reach them through the class name with no `new` needed.

? Which name follows WPILib conventions for a field holding a motor?
- `Motor`
+ `m_motor`
- `kMotor`
- `MOTOR_`
> `m_` is for member fields, and `k` is for constants.

docs.title: Lambdas: code you hand to someone else
docs.text:
A lambda is a method with no name that you can store in a variable and pass around. It's written () -> something. The () holds any inputs, and the arrow points to the code to run.

This matters in FRC because you often want to say "do this, but not right now, do it when the driver presses a button." Passing m_motor.set(0.5) directly would run it immediately, when the code is read. Wrapping it as () -> m_motor.set(0.5) gives the scheduler a package to run later.

Lambdas are mainly used in button bindings, where Java expects a runnable, and passing it a method with a parameter instead will confuse it.

//@ title: Running code later
//@ goal: Run it. The counter only changes when run() is called, not when the lambda is created. Add a third call to run().
//@ lines: 12
public class Counter {
    public int value = 0;
}

Counter counter = new Counter();
Runnable addOne = () -> counter.value++;

System.out.println("Before: " + counter.value);
addOne.run();
addOne.run();
System.out.println("After: " + counter.value);

A lambda that gives something back is called a supplier. DoubleSupplier gives back a double, and BooleanSupplier gives back a boolean. Joystick values are a classic use. Pushing the stick changes the value, so you can't just read it once. You pass a supplier that reads it fresh each time.

//@ title: A snapshot vs a live value
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: What do the two lines print?
//@ lines: 12
public class Joystick {
    public double y = 0.0;
}

Joystick stick = new Joystick();

double snapshot = stick.y;            // reads the value once, right now
DoubleSupplier live = () -> stick.y;  // reads the value every time it's asked

stick.y = 0.8;

System.out.println("snapshot: " + snapshot);
System.out.println("live: " + live.getAsDouble());
//@@ explain
`snapshot` was copied while the stick was still at 0.0 and never changes. The lambda `live` looks at the stick when asked, so it sees 0.8. This is exactly why drive commands take `() -> controller.getLeftY()` instead of `controller.getLeftY()`.

Finally, you'll sometimes see this::method or m_intake::isReady. That's a method reference, shorthand for a lambda that does nothing but call that method: m_intake::isReady means the same as () -> m_intake.isReady().

@ title: Lambdas
? What does `() -> m_motor.set(0.5)` do when Java reaches it?
- Sets the motor to 0.5 immediately
+ Creates a package of code to be run later, without running it yet
- Throws an error
- Sets the motor to 0.5 for 20 ms
> A lambda is just code waiting to be run. Calling it (or having the scheduler call it) is what runs it.

? Which one passes a __live__ joystick reading to a drive command?
- `controller.getLeftY()`
+ `() -> controller.getLeftY()`
- `getLeftY`
- `controller.getLeftY`
> The lambda is a `DoubleSupplier` that gets asked for the latest value every loop.

? `m_intake::isReady` is shorthand for which lambda?
- `() -> m_intake`
+ `() -> m_intake.isReady()`
- `m_intake -> isReady`
- `() -> isReady`
> A method reference is a shortcut for a lambda that only calls that method.

docs.title: Interfaces: a promise about what a class can do
docs.text:
An interface is a list of methods with no code inside them. A class that implements the interface promises to write every one of those methods. Anything that wants to use the class only has to know about the interface, not which class is behind it.

This solves a real robot problem. The same mechanism has to work in three places: on the robot (talking to a real motor), in simulation (a pretend motor), and when we replay a match log on a laptop (no motor at all). So we write one interface for the mechanism, then one class per place.

//@ title: One interface, two classes
//@ goal: Run it. Then change the single line that says new ShooterIOSim() to new ShooterIOReal() and run it again. Only that one line changes, but the behavior does.
//@ lines: 22
public interface ShooterIO {
    void setVoltage(double volts);
}

public class ShooterIOReal implements ShooterIO {
    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double volts) {
        System.out.println("Real motor spinning at " + volts + " V");
    }
}

public class ShooterIOSim implements ShooterIO {
    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double volts) {
        System.out.println("Pretend motor spinning at " + volts + " V");
    }
}

ShooterIO io = new ShooterIOSim();
io.setVoltage(6.0);

Look at the variable's type. It's ShooterIO, the promise, not ShooterIOSim, the actual class. That's what lets you swap one class for another without changing any code that uses io. A subsystem holds a ShooterIO and never knows or cares which one it was given.

Now write one yourself. When we replay a log, the data comes from the file, so there is no hardware to command. The replay class implements every method and does nothing.

//@ title: Write the replay class
//@ goal: Add a class named ShooterIOReplay that implements ShooterIO. Its setVoltage method should do nothing at all.
//@ lines: 18
//@ require: class\s+ShooterIOReplay\s+implements\s+ShooterIO | Declare class ShooterIOReplay implements ShooterIO.
//@ require: @Override | Mark setVoltage with @Override.
public interface ShooterIO {
    void setVoltage(double volts);
}

public class ShooterIOSim implements ShooterIO {
    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double volts) {
        System.out.println("Pretend motor spinning at " + volts + " V");
    }
}

// Write ShooterIOReplay here:

//@@ harness
ShooterIO io = new ShooterIOReplay();
io.setVoltage(6.0);
System.out.println("no hardware touched");
//@@ expect
no hardware touched
//@@ hint
The first line is `public class ShooterIOReplay implements ShooterIO {`
//@@ hint
Inside, copy the method header from the interface, add `@Override` above it, and give it an empty body: `{ }`
//@@ solution
public class ShooterIOReplay implements ShooterIO {
    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double volts) {}
}
//@@ explain
An empty method is a perfectly good implementation. The subsystem calls `setVoltage` like always, and in a replay nothing happens, because the logged data already says what the motor did.
@ title: Interfaces
? What does an interface contain?
- All the code for a mechanism
+ A list of methods a class must provide, without the code
- Only constants
- A copy of another class
> An interface says __what__ a class can do. The classes that implement it say __how__.

? A class says `implements ShooterIO` but forgets to write one of the interface's methods. What happens?
- It runs, and the missing method does nothing
+ Java refuses to compile it
- Java writes the missing method for you
- The robot crashes only when that method is called
> Java checks the promise before the program ever runs.

? Why does the Shooter subsystem hold a `ShooterIO` instead of a `ShooterIOSim`?
- `ShooterIO` runs faster
+ So any class that implements `ShooterIO` can be handed in: real, sim or replay
- Because `ShooterIOSim` is private
- It doesn't matter, they're the same thing
> Holding the interface type is what makes the classes swappable.

docs.title: Enums: a fixed list of named choices
docs.text:
An enum is a type that can only be one of a short list of names that you define. We use them for states: what a mechanism is currently doing.

An enum
public enum IntakeState {
    kStow,
    kIntaking,
    kOuttaking
}

A variable of type IntakeState can hold IntakeState.kStow, IntakeState.kIntaking or IntakeState.kOuttaking, and nothing else. The names start with k like our constants.

Why not just use a String, like "intaking"? Because strings can be misspelled. "intakng" compiles without a complaint and then does nothing. Misspell an enum name and Java refuses to compile, which is exactly where you want the mistake caught.

//@ title: Using an enum
//@ goal: Run it. Then change the state to kOuttaking and run it again. Then try misspelling a state name and read the error.
//@ lines: 20
public enum IntakeState {
    kStow,
    kIntaking,
    kOuttaking
}

IntakeState state = IntakeState.kIntaking;

System.out.println("State is " + state);

if (state == IntakeState.kStow) {
    System.out.println("Rollers off");
}

switch (state) {
    case kIntaking:
        System.out.println("Rollers pulling in");
        break;
    case kOuttaking:
        System.out.println("Rollers pushing out");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Nothing to do");
        break;
}

Two things to notice. Compare enums with ==, because there is only ever one kStow. And in a switch on an enum, the cases are written without the type name (case kIntaking:, not case IntakeState.kIntaking:).

//@ title: Write an enum
//@ goal: Write an enum named ElevatorState with three states: kStow, kScoring and kIntaking.
//@ lines: 8
//@ require: enum\s+ElevatorState | Declare an enum named ElevatorState.
// Write your enum here:

//@@ harness
ElevatorState s = ElevatorState.kScoring;
System.out.println(s);
System.out.println(ElevatorState.values().length);
//@@ expect
kScoring
3
//@@ hint
The pattern is `public enum Name { kOne, kTwo, kThree }`, with commas between the names.
//@@ solution
public enum ElevatorState {
    kStow,
    kScoring,
    kIntaking
}
//@@ explain
Printing an enum shows its name. `values()` gives back every state in the enum, so `values().length` is how many there are.
@ title: Enums
? Which line is a valid use of an enum called `ArmState`?
- `ArmState s = "kStow";`
- `ArmState s = 3;`
+ `ArmState s = ArmState.kStow;`
- `ArmState s = new kStow();`
> An enum variable holds one of the enum's named values, written `TypeName.kName`.

? What is the main reason to use an enum instead of a `String` for a state?
- Enums use less memory
+ A misspelled enum name is a compile error, but a misspelled string silently does the wrong thing
- Strings can't be compared
- Enums run faster on the roboRIO
> Catching the typo before the robot runs saves a lot of debugging.

docs.title: Maps: looking something up
docs.text:
A map stores pairs: a key and the value that goes with it. You give it the key and get the value back, like looking up a word in a dictionary. You write its types in angle brackets as Map<KeyType, ValueType>.

//@ title: A map of speeds
//@ goal: Run it. Then add a "turbo" entry with a speed of 1.0 and print it.
//@ lines: 14
Map<String, Double> speeds = new HashMap<>();

speeds.put("slow", 0.3);
speeds.put("normal", 0.6);

System.out.println(speeds.get("slow"));
System.out.println(speeds.get("normal"));
System.out.println(speeds.getOrDefault("turbo", 0.0));
System.out.println(speeds.containsKey("normal"));

put adds a pair, get looks one up, and getOrDefault gives a backup answer when the key isn't there. If you get a key that was never added, you get null, and calling anything on null crashes the program. Remember that, because it's the source of the most common mistake in the next exercise.

Here's where it gets useful. A map's value can be a piece of code: a Runnable is a lambda that takes nothing and gives nothing back. So a Map<IntakeState, Runnable> says, "for each state, here's what to run." And the shorthand this::stowPeriodic is a method reference, which you met above, meaning "the method called stowPeriodic on this object."

Predict what this does. Follow the state through each call.

//@ title: A map of what to do
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: Four calls to periodic(), with the mode changing in between. What does it print?
//@ lines: 28
public enum Mode {
    kSlow,
    kFast
}

public class Driver {
    private Map<Mode, Runnable> m_actions = new HashMap<>();
    private Mode m_mode = Mode.kSlow;

    public Driver() {
        m_actions.put(Mode.kSlow, this::slow);
        m_actions.put(Mode.kFast, this::fast);
    }

    public void setMode(Mode mode) { m_mode = mode; }

    public void periodic() { m_actions.get(m_mode).run(); }

    private void slow() { System.out.println("creeping"); }
    private void fast() { System.out.println("flying"); }
}

Driver d = new Driver();
d.periodic();
d.setMode(Mode.kFast);
d.periodic();
d.periodic();
d.setMode(Mode.kSlow);
d.periodic();
//@@ explain
`periodic()` looks up the method registered for the current mode and runs it. Changing the mode never runs anything by itself, it only changes which method the __next__ `periodic()` will pick. This exact pattern runs every subsystem on our robot.

Now finish one yourself. This arm only registered one of its two states, so asking it to reach crashes.

//@ title: Register the missing state
//@ goal: Run it and read the error. Then register kReach with this::reachPeriodic so the arm can reach.
//@ lines: 24
//@ require: put\(\s*ArmState\.kReach\s*,\s*this::reachPeriodic\s*\) | Register kReach with this::reachPeriodic.
public enum ArmState {
    kStow,
    kReach
}

public class Arm {
    private ArmState m_state = ArmState.kStow;
    private Map<ArmState, Runnable> m_periodic = new HashMap<>();

    public Arm() {
        m_periodic.put(ArmState.kStow, this::stowPeriodic);
        // Register kReach here
    }

    public void setState(ArmState state) { m_state = state; }

    public void periodic() { m_periodic.get(m_state).run(); }

    private void stowPeriodic() { System.out.println("arm down"); }
    private void reachPeriodic() { System.out.println("arm up"); }
}
//@@ harness
Arm arm = new Arm();
arm.periodic();
arm.setState(ArmState.kReach);
arm.periodic();
//@@ expect
arm down
arm up
//@@ hint
The line for kStow is already there. Add one just like it for kReach.
//@@ hint

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
You now know how a robot program runs, where things live, and the Java that holds it together: interfaces, enums, and maps of methods. Those three ideas are exactly how our subsystems are built. Next you will build the pieces:

  • Subsystems: split a mechanism into an IO interface, real and simulated IO classes, and a subsystem that runs on states.
  • RobotContainer: build every subsystem, pick real or simulated hardware, and connect the controller.
  • RobotState: the robot's brain, which turns "the driver pressed intake" into the right state for every subsystem.
  • Constants: where every number lives, and how to tune it while the robot runs.

docs.title: RobotContainer
docs.text:
If subsystems are the parts of the robot, RobotContainer is where the parts get assembled. It builds every subsystem, picks whether they talk to real or simulated hardware, creates the controllers, and connects each button to something that happens.

A good way to think about it

Subsystems know how. Intake knows how to run its rollers. RobotContainer builds what exists. It creates the intake and hands it the right IO class. The buttons decide when. Pressing A tells the robot to start intaking.

RobotContainer should contain very little real logic. It reads almost like a list of instructions, and that's a good thing. If you find yourself writing math in here, it probably belongs in a subsystem.

docs.title: Four steps, in order
docs.text:
Our RobotContainer has a constructor that does the same four things every year, each in its own method.

RobotContainer.java
public RobotContainer() {
    configureSubsystems();     // build the subsystems, real or sim
    configureCommands();       // the autonomous chooser and its routines
    configureControllers();    // which controller is plugged in
    configureButtonBindings(); // what each button does
}

The order matters. Bindings need the controllers, and the controllers' buttons need the subsystems to point at. We'll go through them in a slightly different order, starting with the most surprising one.

docs.title: Real, sim or replay?
docs.text:
Remember the three IO classes from Subsystems? RobotContainer is where one of them is chosen. It looks at a setting called the mode and builds each subsystem with the matching IO class.

Constants.java
public static enum Mode {
    REAL,    // running on the robot
    PROTO,   // running on the practice board, with some mechanisms real and some simulated
    SIM,     // running on a laptop, with pretend hardware
    REPLAY   // replaying a log file, with no hardware
}

The mode is set once. When the code is on a roboRIO, WPILib can tell, so kCurrentMode is REAL there and SIM everywhere else. To replay a log, we change it by hand. Then configureSubsystems() is one big switch:

configureSubsystems(), shortened
switch (Constants.kCurrentMode) {
    case REAL:
        m_intake = new Intake(new IntakeRollerIOKraken(Ports.kIntakeRoller), ...);
        break;
    case SIM:
        m_intake = new Intake(new IntakeRollerIOSim(), ...);
        break;
    case REPLAY:
        m_intake = new Intake(new IntakeRollerIOReplay(), ...);
        break;
}

That switch is the only place that decides which IO class each subsystem is connected to. (A few other spots check the mode too, such as Robot.java choosing where to send the logs, but none of them choose the hardware.) Try it. Here's the full intake with a mode switch. Run it, switch to Teleop, press A, and look at the dashboard. Then change kCurrentMode to Mode.REAL, press Restart, and press A again. A motor shows up, because now IntakeIOKraken is the class being used. Then try Mode.REPLAY: nothing responds at all, because that class does nothing.

docs.title: Bindings: buttons change states
docs.text:
A Trigger is a button (or any true/false condition) that can start things when it changes. Here are the ways to react to it:

Method When it happens onTrue(command) Once, at the moment the button goes down. onFalse(command) Once, at the moment the button is released. whileTrue(command) While the button is held. It's cancelled on release.

Since our subsystems have states instead of commands, a binding wraps a state change in Commands.runOnce. runOnce takes a lambda, a package of code, and makes a command that runs it one time and finishes.

m_driverControls.coralIntake().onTrue(
    Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(IntakeState.kIntaking)));

Read it as: "when the intake button goes down, run this one line, which sets the intake's state." Nothing happens right then except the state change. The next periodic() does the rest.
