        m_driver.a().onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kIntaking)));

        m_driver.b()
            .onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kOuttaking)))
            .onFalse(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kStow)));
    }

    public Intake getIntake() {
        return m_intake;
    }
}
//@@ explain
`onTrue` handles the press and `onFalse` handles the release. Without `onFalse`, the intake would keep outtaking forever once you let go.

A lesson from our own code

You may find toggleOnTrue, a WPILib binding that starts something on the first press and stops it on the next. Our RobotContainer doesn't use it. A comment in the code says, "if anyone is reading this, here's a lesson: don't use WPILib toggle, it's not good." Our intake button instead sets a robot action through RobotState and watches that action, so the button always matches what the robot is really doing. You'll see how on the RobotState page.

docs.title: Bindings that call RobotState
docs.text:
The intake button above is a simplification. On the real robot, one button press usually changes several subsystems at once, so the binding doesn't call a subsystem. It tells RobotState what the robot should be doing.

A real binding from our RobotContainer
m_driverControls
    .coralEject()
    .onTrue(
        Commands.runOnce(
            () -> {
              RobotState.getInstance().updateRobotAction(RobotAction.kCoralEject);
            }))
    .onFalse(
        Commands.runOnce(
            () -> {
              RobotState.getInstance().setDefaultAction();
            }));

Same shape as the B button: something on press, something else on release. It just talks to a different object. The next page explains it.

docs.title: Zeroing while the robot is disabled
docs.text:
Commands don't run while the robot is disabled, which is a safety feature. But some things you want to do before a match, while disabled, like telling the elevator "this is height zero." Our code adds .ignoringDisable(true) to those bindings.

m_driverControls
    .zeroElevator()
    .onTrue(
        Commands.runOnce(() -> m_elevator.zeroElevator())
            .ignoringDisable(true));

Try it. This container is set to disabled before the button is pressed, so the zero command is silently ignored.

//@ title: Zero while disabled
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: Pressing START should zero the elevator even while the robot is disabled. Right now it does nothing. Fix the binding.
//@ lines: 22
//@ require: ignoringDisable\(\s*true\s*\) | Add .ignoringDisable(true) to the command.
public class Elevator {
    private int m_zeroCount = 0;

    public void zero() { m_zeroCount++; }

    public int getZeroCount() { return m_zeroCount; }
}

public class RobotContainer {
    private final Elevator m_elevator = new Elevator();
    private final CommandXboxController m_driver = new CommandXboxController(0);

    public RobotContainer() {
        m_driver.start().onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_elevator.zero()));
    }

    public Elevator getElevator() {
        return m_elevator;
    }
}
//@@ harness
Sim.setMode("disabled");
RobotContainer container = new RobotContainer();
Sim.press(0, "START");
Sim.loops(2);
System.out.println(container.getElevator().getZeroCount());
//@@ expect
1
//@@ hint
Add one call onto the end of `Commands.runOnce(...)`, before the closing parenthesis of `onTrue`.
//@@ solution
public class Elevator {
    private int m_zeroCount = 0;

    public void zero() { m_zeroCount++; }

    public int getZeroCount() { return m_zeroCount; }
}

public class RobotContainer {
    private final Elevator m_elevator = new Elevator();
    private final CommandXboxController m_driver = new CommandXboxController(0);

    public RobotContainer() {
        m_driver.start().onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_elevator.zero()).ignoringDisable(true));
    }

    public Elevator getElevator() {
        return m_elevator;
    }
}
//@@ explain
Commands don't run when the robot is disabled unless you say they may. Zeroing a sensor is exactly the kind of thing you want to do before the match starts.

docs.title: Driving: the default command
docs.text:
Driving is where we do use commands. Most subsystems sit idle until a button asks for them, but the drivetrain should respond to the sticks all the time. So it gets a default command: the command that runs whenever nothing else is using that subsystem.

Driving commands live in commands/drive/DriveCommands.java as static methods, not inside the subsystem. They take their inputs as suppliers, the live lambdas from FRC Nuances, so they read the sticks fresh every loop. Notice m_driverControls::getForward, a method reference, passed in where a live value is needed.

//@ title: A drivetrain with a default command
//@ panel: robot
//@ show: controller,motors,dashboard
//@ goal: Run it, switch to Teleop, and drive: left stick up for forward, right stick sideways to turn. Then remove the minus sign in getTurn() and see which way it turns.
//@ lines: 60
//@ maxlines: 34
public class Drive extends SubsystemBase {
    private final TalonFX m_left = new TalonFX(1);
    private final TalonFX m_right = new TalonFX(2);
    private final DifferentialDrive m_drive = new DifferentialDrive(m_left, m_right);

    public void arcadeDrive(double forward, double turn) {
        m_drive.arcadeDrive(forward, turn);
    }
}

public class DriveCommands {
    private DriveCommands() {}

    public static Command arcade(Drive drive, DoubleSupplier forward, DoubleSupplier turn) {
        return Commands.run(
            () -> drive.arcadeDrive(forward.getAsDouble(), turn.getAsDouble()),
            drive);
    }
}

public interface DriverControls {
    double getForward();

    double getTurn();
}

public class DriverControlsXbox implements DriverControls {
    private final CommandXboxController m_controller = new CommandXboxController(0);

    @Override
    public double getForward() {
        return -m_controller.getLeftY();
    }

    @Override
    public double getTurn() {
        return -m_controller.getRightX();
    }
}

public class RobotContainer {
    private final Drive m_drive = new Drive();
    private final DriverControls m_driverControls = new DriverControlsXbox();

    public RobotContainer() {
        m_drive.setDefaultCommand(
            DriveCommands.arcade(m_drive, m_driverControls::getForward, m_driverControls::getTurn));
    }
}

Our real drivetrain is a swerve drive, which is a lot more math, but it hooks up the same way: a joystickDrive command is set as the drivetrain's default command, fed by getForward, getStrafe and getTurn.

@ title: Controllers and driving
? Why does `getForward()` return `-m_controller.getLeftY()`?
- The controller is broken
+ Pushing a stick forward reads negative, so the controller class flips it once, in one place
- Negative numbers are faster
- WPILib requires it
> Forward is negative on Y. Flipping it inside the controller class means nobody else has to remember.

? Why do drive commands take `m_driverControls::getForward` instead of `m_driverControls.getForward()`?
- It runs faster
+ The command needs to read the stick again on every loop, not once
- Java requires method references for suppliers
- To hide the controller
> Without a supplier you'd capture the stick's value at one instant and the robot would never respond to it moving.

? Which statement about a default command is true?
- It runs once when the robot turns on
+ It runs whenever nothing else is using that subsystem
- It makes the subsystem ignore other commands
- Every subsystem must have one
> It's perfect for driving. Pressing a button that needs the drivetrain interrupts it, and it resumes afterwards.

docs.title: Autonomous: getAutonomousCommand()
docs.text:
During autonomous nobody touches the controllers, so the robot runs a pre-planned routine. In code, a routine is just one command, usually several small ones chained together. RobotContainer hands it over in getAutonomousCommand(), and Robot.java schedules it when autonomous starts.

Because our subsystems run on states, an autonomous step is often just "set a state," then wait. Two helpers chain the steps:

  • Commands.waitSeconds(seconds) does nothing for that long.
  • Commands.sequence(a, b, c) runs a, then b, then c.

Here is a complete example, Robot.java included. Run it, switch to Auto, and watch Intake/State. It intakes for a second and then stows by itself. Switch to Teleop and any unfinished autonomous command is cancelled.

//@ title: A simple autonomous
//@ panel: robot
//@ show: dashboard,scheduler
//@ goal: Run it and switch to Auto: the intake runs for 1 second, then stows. Change the wait, or add a second step.
//@ lines: 110
//@ maxlines: 34
public interface IntakeIO {
    @AutoLog
    public static class IntakeInputs {
        public double velocityRPS;
        public double voltage;
    }

    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs);

    public void setVoltage(double voltage);
}

public class IntakeIOSim implements IntakeIO {
    private double m_voltage = 0.0;
    private double m_velocity = 0.0;

    @Override
    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs) {
        m_velocity += (m_voltage * 8.0 - m_velocity) * 0.2;
        inputs.velocityRPS = m_velocity;
        inputs.voltage = m_voltage;
    }

    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double voltage) {
        m_voltage = voltage;
    }
}

public class Intake extends SubsystemBase {
    public static enum IntakeState {
        kStow,
        kIntaking,
        kOuttaking
    }

    private final IntakeIO m_io;
    private final IntakeInputsAutoLogged m_inputs = new IntakeInputsAutoLogged();
    private final SubsystemProfiles<IntakeState> m_profiles;

    public Intake(IntakeIO io) {
        m_io = io;

        Map<IntakeState, Runnable> periodicHash = new HashMap<>();
        periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kStow, this::stowPeriodic);
        periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kIntaking, this::intakingPeriodic);
        periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kOuttaking, this::outtakingPeriodic);

        m_profiles = new SubsystemProfiles<>(periodicHash, IntakeState.kStow);
    }

    public void updateState(IntakeState state) {
        m_profiles.setCurrentProfile(state);
    }

    public IntakeState getCurrentState() {
        return m_profiles.getCurrentProfile();
    }

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        m_io.updateInputs(m_inputs);
        m_profiles.getPeriodicFunctionTimed().run();
        Logger.processInputs("Intake", m_inputs);
        Logger.recordOutput("Intake/State", m_profiles.getCurrentProfile());
    }

    public void stowPeriodic() {
        m_io.setVoltage(0.0);
    }

    public void intakingPeriodic() {
        m_io.setVoltage(8.0);
    }

    public void outtakingPeriodic() {
        m_io.setVoltage(-8.0);
    }
}

public class RobotContainer {
    private final Intake m_intake = new Intake(new IntakeIOSim());

    public Command getAutonomousCommand() {
        return Commands.sequence(
            Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kIntaking)),
            Commands.waitSeconds(1.0),
            Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kStow)));
    }
}

public class Robot extends LoggedRobot {
    private final RobotContainer m_robotContainer;
    private Command m_autonomousCommand;

    public Robot() {
        m_robotContainer = new RobotContainer();
    }

    @Override
    public void robotPeriodic() {
        CommandScheduler.getInstance().run();
    }

    @Override
    public void autonomousInit() {
        m_autonomousCommand = m_robotContainer.getAutonomousCommand();
        if (m_autonomousCommand != null) {
            m_autonomousCommand.schedule();
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void teleopInit() {
        if (m_autonomousCommand != null) {
            m_autonomousCommand.cancel();
        }
    }
}

On the real robot there isn't one routine, there's a menu. RobotContainer builds a chooser the drivers use on the dashboard, and getAutonomousCommand() returns whichever was picked.

configureCommands(), shortened
m_autoChooser = new LoggedDashboardChooser<>("Auto Chooser");
m_autoFactory = new AutoFactory(m_drive);

m_autoChooser.addOption("Do Nothing", Commands.none());
m_autoChooser.addDefaultOption("3 Coral Left", m_autoFactory.getAutoCommand("3 Coral Left"));

// every path drawn in PathPlanner shows up as an option too
for (String path : PathPlannerUtil.getExistingPaths()) {
    m_autoChooser.addOption(path, m_autoFactory.getAutoCommand(path));
}
getAutonomousCommand()
public Command getAutonomousCommand() {
    return m_autoChooser.get();
}

AutoFactory also teaches PathPlanner the names of our actions, like "Set Height L1", each one a Commands.runOnce that sets something in RobotState. So a routine drawn in PathPlanner can say "drive here, set L1, score" and the same state machine does the work.

Now build one. Make this routine intake for 2 seconds, then outtake for 1 second, then stow.

//@ title: Build an autonomous routine
//@ prelude: wpilib
//@ goal: Build the routine: intake for 2 seconds, outtake for 1 second, then stow. Use Commands.sequence, runOnce and waitSeconds.
//@ lines: 36
//@ maxlines: 30
//@ require: waitSeconds | Use Commands.waitSeconds(...) for the waiting.
//@ require: sequence|andThen | Chain the steps with Commands.sequence(...) or andThen(...).
public class Intake {
    public static enum IntakeState {
        kStow,
        kIntaking,
        kOuttaking
    }

    private IntakeState m_state = IntakeState.kStow;

    public void updateState(IntakeState state) {
        m_state = state;
    }

    public IntakeState getCurrentState() {
        return m_state;
    }
}

public class RobotContainer {
    private final Intake m_intake = new Intake();

    public Command getAutonomousCommand() {
        // Build the routine here
        return Commands.none();
    }

    public Intake getIntake() {
        return m_intake;
    }
}
//@@ harness
RobotContainer container = new RobotContainer();
container.getAutonomousCommand().schedule();
Sim.loops(10);
System.out.println(container.getIntake().getCurrentState());
Sim.loops(110);
System.out.println(container.getIntake().getCurrentState());
Sim.loops(80);
System.out.println(container.getIntake().getCurrentState());
//@@ expect
kIntaking
kOuttaking
kStow
//@@ hint
The routine is five steps: set intaking, wait, set outtaking, wait, set stow.
//@@ hint
Each "set" is `Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kIntaking))` with a different state. Each wait is `Commands.waitSeconds(2.0)`.
//@@ solution
public class Intake {
    public static enum IntakeState {
        kStow,
        kIntaking,
        kOuttaking
    }

    private IntakeState m_state = IntakeState.kStow;

    public void updateState(IntakeState state) {
        m_state = state;
    }

    public IntakeState getCurrentState() {
        return m_state;
    }
}

public class RobotContainer {
    private final Intake m_intake = new Intake();

    public Command getAutonomousCommand() {
        return Commands.sequence(
            Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kIntaking)),
            Commands.waitSeconds(2.0),
            Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kOuttaking)),
            Commands.waitSeconds(1.0),
            Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kStow)));
    }

    public Intake getIntake() {
        return m_intake;
    }
}
//@@ explain
An autonomous routine is a timeline of state changes. The subsystems do the actual work in their `periodic()` methods, the same as in teleop.

docs.title: What belongs where?
docs.text:
Now that you've seen every part of RobotContainer, test your sense of where things go.

@ title: RobotContainer
? Which of these belongs in `RobotContainer`?
- The code that sets the intake motor's voltage
+ The line that makes the A button change the intake's state
- The intake motor's CAN id
- The code that calls `periodic()` on each subsystem
> Subsystems hold the "how", constants hold the numbers, and `RobotContainer` connects the buttons.

? Which file is the only one that needs to change when the team moves "outtake" from the B button to the Y button?
- `Intake.java`
- `RobotContainer.java`
+ `DriverControlsXbox.java`
- `Constants.java`
> `RobotContainer` asks for `outtake()`. Which button that is lives in the controller class.

? A button binding for "hold to run, release to stop" needs:
- Only `onTrue`
+ `onTrue` for the press and `onFalse` for the release
- `toggleOnTrue`
- Nothing, it's automatic
> Without `onFalse`, nothing ever tells the mechanism to stop.

? You want a button to zero the elevator before a match, while the robot is still disabled. What must you add?
- `.onFalse(...)`
+ `.ignoringDisable(true)` on the command
- `.whileTrue(...)`
- Nothing, commands always run
> Commands don't run while disabled unless they say they may.

? When does `Robot.java` ask `RobotContainer` for the autonomous command?
- When the robot is first powered on
+ When autonomous mode starts
- Every 20 ms
- When teleop starts
> `autonomousInit()` calls `getAutonomousCommand()` and schedules whatever comes back.

? Pushing the left stick forward reads...
- +1.0
+ -1.0
- 0.0
- It depends on the controller's batteries
> Forward is negative on Y, which is why the controller class negates it.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: You've seen how the robot is assembled and how buttons reach it. The last piece is what happens when a button is pressed and several subsystems need to change together. That's the job of RobotState.

docs.title: RobotState
docs.text:
Say the driver presses one button: intake. Think about everything that has to happen. The intake rollers spin. The indexer starts moving the game piece along. The elevator drops to the pickup height. Three subsystems, one button.

Where does the code that coordinates them go?

  • In the button binding? Then every button needs a long list of subsystem calls, and the same list gets copied anywhere else the robot intakes, like in autonomous.
  • In a subsystem? Then the intake has to know about the elevator, and the elevator has to know about the indexer. Our subsystems are built so each one only knows about itself.

Our answer is a class called RobotState. It sits above all the subsystems and keeps track of one thing: what is the robot trying to do right now?

Two levels of state

Subsystem states say what one mechanism is doing: the intake is kIntaking. Robot actions say what the whole robot is doing: the robot is kCoralIntaking. One action sets a state for every subsystem it needs.

graph TD
    B["Driver presses a button"] -->|"updateRobotAction(kCoralIntaking)"| RS["RobotState<br>the current action"]
    RS -->|"updateState(kIntaking)"| I["Intake"]
    RS -->|"updateState(kIndexing)"| X["Indexer"]
    RS -->|"updateState(kIntaking)"| E["Elevator"]

You've already used the idea twice. A subsystem is an enum of states plus a map from each state to the method that runs. RobotState does the same thing one level up, with an enum of actions.

docs.title: RobotAction: what the robot is trying to do
docs.text:
Here are a few of the actions from our 2025 robot.

RobotState.java
public enum RobotAction {
    kTeleopDefault,   // nothing special: everything rests
    kCoralIntaking,   // get a game piece into the robot
    kCoralOuttaking,  // release the game piece we're holding
    kAutoScore,       // drive to the reef and score on our own
    kManualScore,     // raise the elevator, driver lines up
    kCoralEject,      // spit the game piece back out
    // ...about twenty more
}

Each one is a goal, not a motor setting. kCoralIntaking doesn't say how fast anything spins. It says what we're trying to do, and each subsystem knows how to do its part.

docs.title: One instance for the whole robot
docs.text:
Any button, anywhere, needs to be able to say "change the robot's action." So there is exactly one RobotState, and any file can get it by calling RobotState.getInstance(). A class that only ever has one object is called a singleton, and it's built from things you already know: static and private.

RobotState.java
public class RobotState {
    private static RobotState m_instance;

    private RobotState(Drive drive, Intake intake, Indexer indexer, /* ... */) {
        // ...save the subsystems, build the map of actions...
    }

    public static RobotState startInstance(Drive drive, Intake intake, Indexer indexer, /* ... */) {
        if (m_instance == null) {
            m_instance = new RobotState(drive, intake, indexer, /* ... */);
        }
        return m_instance;
    }

    public static RobotState getInstance() {
        return m_instance;
    }
}
  • The constructor is private, so nobody else can write new RobotState(...).
  • m_instance is static, so it belongs to the class itself and is shared by everyone.
  • startInstance builds it once, at startup. It needs the subsystems, so it can only run after RobotContainer has created them. That's why configureCommands() in our RobotContainer calls it, with a comment saying "we start here so autofactory won't be null".
  • After that, everyone calls getInstance().

Predict what this prints. Pay attention to what a == b asks Java: not "do they look the same?" but "are they the very same object?"

//@ title: One object, shared
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: Both calls to getInstance() happen in different places. Type the two lines this prints.
//@ lines: 18
public class Config {
    private static Config m_instance;
    private int m_value = 0;

    private Config() {}

    public static Config getInstance() {
        if (m_instance == null) {
            m_instance = new Config();
        }
        return m_instance;
    }

    public void add(int amount) { m_value += amount; }
    public int get() { return m_value; }
}

Config.getInstance().add(5);
Config.getInstance().add(2);

Config a = Config.getInstance();
Config b = Config.getInstance();
System.out.println(a.get());
System.out.println(a == b);
//@@ expect
7
true
//@@ explain
There's only one `Config`. Both `add` calls changed the same object, so its value is 7, and `a` and `b` are two names for that one object. This is how a button binding and an autonomous routine can both talk to the same `RobotState`.

docs.title: Changing the action
docs.text:
Every button that changes what the robot is doing ends up calling one method: updateRobotAction. It follows the same three steps every time.

updateRobotAction(), shortened
public void updateRobotAction(RobotAction newAction) {
    // 1. Start every subsystem at its resting state
    IntakeState newIntakeState = IntakeState.kStow;
    IndexerState newIndexerState = IndexerState.kIdle;
    ElevatorState newElevatorState = ElevatorState.kStow;

    // 2. Let the action change the ones it cares about
    switch (newAction) {
        case kCoralIntaking:
            newIntakeState = IntakeState.kFunnelIntaking;
            newElevatorState = ElevatorState.kIntaking;
            break;

        case kManualScore:
            newElevatorState = ElevatorState.kScoring;
            break;

        case kTeleopDefault:
            break;
    }

    // 3. Remember the action, then tell each subsystem, but only if its state is changing
    m_profiles.setCurrentProfile(newAction);

    if (m_intake.getCurrentState() != newIntakeState) {
        m_intake.updateState(newIntakeState);
    }
    if (m_indexer.getCurrentState() != newIndexerState) {
        m_indexer.updateState(newIndexerState);
    }
    if (m_elevator.getCurrentState() != newElevatorState) {
        m_elevator.updateState(newElevatorState);
    }
}

Step 1 is the clever one. Because everything starts at "rest," an action only has to list what is different. Switching from intaking to the default action puts everything back without a single line of cleanup. Nothing gets left running by accident.

Step 3 only updates a subsystem when its state is actually changing, so we don't restart a motion that's already going.

A small honesty note: for some subsystems, "rest" depends on what's happening. Our real code doesn't start the intake at kStow but at m_intake.getStowOrHold(), which stays in the hold state if the intake is already holding a game piece, and only stows otherwise. The idea is the same: start from a default, then let the action change it.

A switch needs a break

Each case ends with break. Without it, Java keeps running into the next case. Our code has a comment on this: "guys don't use fallthrough it's not worth it". Two cases that do the same thing can share a body by being stacked (case kAutoScore: directly above case kAutoAutoScore:), but any case with code in it ends in break.

Here is the whole thing running. The button bindings are one-liners, just like the real RobotContainer. Run it, switch to Teleop, and press A (intake), B (score), and X (back to default). Watch three subsystems change together on the dashboard. The DIO 0 button is a pretend sensor that says "we have a game piece."

//@ title: One button, three subsystems
//@ panel: robot
//@ show: controller,motors,dashboard
//@ dio: 0
//@ goal: Run it, go to Teleop, and press A. The intake and indexer start together. Then press DIO 0 (we have a piece): the indexer stops by itself. Press B to score, then X for default.
//@ lines: 120
//@ maxlines: 36
public class Intake extends SubsystemBase {
    public static enum IntakeState { kStow, kIntaking }

    private final TalonFX m_motor = new TalonFX(1);
    private IntakeState m_state = IntakeState.kStow;

    public void updateState(IntakeState state) { m_state = state; }
    public IntakeState getCurrentState() { return m_state; }

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        m_motor.set(m_state == IntakeState.kIntaking ? 0.7 : 0.0);
        Logger.recordOutput("Intake/State", m_state);
    }
}

public class Indexer extends SubsystemBase {
    public static enum IndexerState { kIdle, kIndexing }

    private final TalonFX m_motor = new TalonFX(2);
    private final DigitalInput m_sensor = new DigitalInput(0);
    private IndexerState m_state = IndexerState.kIdle;

    public void updateState(IndexerState state) { m_state = state; }
    public IndexerState getCurrentState() { return m_state; }
    public boolean hasGamePiece() { return m_sensor.get(); }

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        m_motor.set(m_state == IndexerState.kIndexing ? 0.5 : 0.0);
        Logger.recordOutput("Indexer/State", m_state);
    }
}

public class Elevator extends SubsystemBase {
    public static enum ElevatorState { kStow, kIntaking, kScoring }

    private ElevatorState m_state = ElevatorState.kStow;

    public void updateState(ElevatorState state) { m_state = state; }
    public ElevatorState getCurrentState() { return m_state; }

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        Logger.recordOutput("Elevator/State", m_state);
    }
}

public class RobotState {
    public enum RobotAction { kTeleopDefault, kCoralIntaking, kManualScore }

    private static RobotState m_instance;

    private final Intake m_intake;
    private final Indexer m_indexer;
    private final Elevator m_elevator;
    private final SubsystemProfiles<RobotAction> m_profiles;

        m_indexer = indexer;
        m_elevator = elevator;

        periodicHash.put(RobotAction.kTeleopDefault, () -> {});
        periodicHash.put(RobotAction.kCoralIntaking, this::coralIntakingPeriodic);
        periodicHash.put(RobotAction.kManualScore, () -> {});

        return m_instance;

    public void updateRobotState() {
        m_profiles.getPeriodicFunctionTimed().run();

                newElevatorState = ElevatorState.kIntaking;

                break;

            case kTeleopDefault:
                break;

        if (m_indexer.getCurrentState() != newIndexerState) { m_indexer.updateState(newIndexerState); }

    }

        updateRobotAction(RobotAction.kTeleopDefault);

    public void coralIntakingPeriodic() {
        if (m_indexer.hasGamePiece()) {
            m_indexer.updateState(IndexerState.kIdle);

docs.title: Actions that run code every loop
docs.text:
An action isn't only a set of starting states. Each one can have a method that runs every loop while it's the current action, using the same map-of-methods trick as the subsystems. That's how kCoralIntaking above reacted to the sensor: the indexer stops when the game piece arrives, and starts again if it leaves.

An action can also end itself. Here's how our robot finishes scoring:

coralOuttakingPeriodic(), shortened
public void coralOuttakingPeriodic() {
    // after the game piece has been out for a moment, we're done: go back to rest
    if (m_timer.hasElapsed(ManipulatorConstants.kCoralOuttakeTimeout.get())) {
        setDefaultAction();
    }
    // keep resetting the timer while we still have the game piece
    if (m_manipulator.hasGamePiece() || !m_timer.isRunning()) {
        m_timer.restart();
    }
}

m_timer is a WPILib Timer. The robot is holding the button's goal ("score") until the sensors say it worked. The driver doesn't have to press anything to stop it.

One more detail from the real updateRobotAction: every time the action changes, it also resets the timers and flags. That way a timer left running from the last action can't make the new one end early.

docs.title: Who is allowed to change what?
docs.text:
With three layers, it helps to have a rule for who talks to whom.

  • Buttons (in RobotContainer) ask RobotState for an action. They almost never talk to a subsystem directly.
  • RobotState turns an action into a state for each subsystem.
  • Subsystems run their own state and talk to their own IO. They don't change each other's states.

Our code isn't perfectly strict about it, and that's fine. A subsystem can read RobotState when it needs to know something about the whole robot (our indexer checks whether the manipulator is auto-reversing). A few simple buttons skip it altogether: the climb button flips the climb between two states, and a comment in the code says "this isn't gonna be in robot state because that's too much work."

The rule of thumb: if a button needs more than one subsystem, or needs the robot to remember what it's doing, it goes through RobotState. If it's one mechanism flipping between two states, it can call the subsystem directly.

@ title: RobotState
? Why does `RobotState` exist, instead of each button changing every subsystem it needs?
- Java requires it
+ One place decides what all the subsystems should do together, so buttons and autonomous don't duplicate the lists
- It makes the motors faster
- Subsystems can't have states
> One action can set several subsystems at once, and every button (and autonomous) reuses it.

? What makes `RobotState` a singleton?
- It extends `SubsystemBase`
+ A private constructor and a static instance that everyone gets through `getInstance()`
- It's declared `final`
- It has only one method
> Nobody else can call `new RobotState(...)`, so there can only be the one built by `startInstance`.

? Why does `updateRobotAction` start every subsystem at its resting state before the `switch`?
- To make the code longer
+ So an action only lists what it changes, and nothing from the previous action gets left running
- Because `switch` requires it
- To reset the log file
> Switching back to the default action puts everything at rest with no cleanup code.

? A `case` in the `switch` sets some states but has no `break`. What happens?
- Java reports an error
+ Java keeps running into the next case's code too
- The robot stops
- Nothing, `break` is optional
> That's called fallthrough. Our team avoids it for any case that has code in it.

? When does `RobotState` call each subsystem's `updateState`?
+ When the action changes, in `updateRobotAction`
- Every 20 ms
- Only when the robot is disabled
- Never. The subsystems do it themselves.
> `updateRobotAction` sets them in one go. The action's own periodic method may adjust some every loop.

? In `robotPeriodic()`, which comes first?
- `CommandScheduler.getInstance().run()`
+ `RobotState.getInstance().updateRobotState()`
- Neither. They run at the same time.
- The order doesn't exist, only one runs.
> The robot decides what it's doing first, then the scheduler runs the subsystems.

docs.title: Subsystems
docs.text:
A subsystem is one mechanism on the robot: the intake, the elevator, the climber. On our team, every subsystem is built the same way, in three layers, and it runs on states. Once you've seen one, you can read all of them.

This page builds an intake from scratch. Every editor runs in your browser, so you can try each idea as you read.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text:
The rule is the one from the Java lessons: only one class touches the hardware. Everything else asks. We take that rule one step further and split each mechanism into three layers.

graph TD
    S["Intake.java<br>the subsystem: states and logic"] -->|"only talks to"| IO["IntakeIO.java<br>the interface: what the hardware can do"]
    IO --- K["IntakeIOKraken<br>real motors"]
    IO --- SIM["IntakeIOSim<br>pretend motors"]
    IO --- R["IntakeIOReplay<br>for logged replay"]
  • IntakeIO is an interface. It lists everything the hardware can do (spin at some voltage) and everything it can report (how fast it's spinning).
  • IntakeIOKraken, IntakeIOSim and IntakeIOReplay each implement that interface. One talks to real motors, one is a pretend intake, and one does nothing.
  • Intake is the subsystem. It holds an IntakeIO and never knows which one. All the thinking happens here.

Our real intake is two mechanisms

To keep this page small, we're building an intake with a single roller. On the real robot, the intake is a roller and a pivot arm, so it has two IO folders, intake/roller/ (IntakeRollerIO) and intake/pivot/ (PivotIO), each with its own Kraken, Sim and Replay classes. One Intake subsystem holds both. When you open the real code, that's why you won't find a file called IntakeIO. Every piece works exactly the way it does here, just twice. The Manipulator does the same thing with a roller, a wrist and a sensor.

Why go to all this trouble? Three reasons.

  1. We can test without a robot. The robot isn't always available, and half the team wants to code at the same time. With IntakeIOSim, your code runs on a laptop.
  2. We can replay matches. Every loop, the robot logs everything the hardware reported. After a match, we feed that log back through the same Intake code on a laptop, using the replay class so no hardware is needed, and watch exactly what the code decided. If something went wrong, we can find out why.
  3. Changing hardware touches one file. Swap a motor type and only the Kraken class changes. The logic doesn't care.
graph LR
    subgraph "On the robot"
    A["Real motor"] --> B["IntakeIOKraken"] --> C["Intake logic"] --> L["Log file"]
    end
    subgraph "Replaying on a laptop"
    L2["Log file"] --> D["IntakeIOReplay (no hardware)"] --> E["Same Intake logic"]
    end

Here is the whole thing working. Read it once, press Run, switch to Teleop, then press A (intake), B (outtake) and X (stow). Watch the dashboard on the right. You'll see the state change and the speed ramp up. You will build each of these pieces yourself below.

//@ title: The finished intake
//@ panel: robot
//@ show: controller,dashboard
//@ goal: Run it, switch to Teleop, and press A, B and X. Notice that the speed doesn't jump instantly, because the pretend motor takes a moment to spin up.

public interface IntakeIO {
    @AutoLog
    public static class IntakeInputs {
        public double velocityRPS;
        public double voltage;
    }

    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs);

    public void setVoltage(double voltage);
}

public class IntakeIOSim implements IntakeIO {
    private double m_voltage = 0.0;
    private double m_velocity = 0.0;

    @Override
    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs) {
        // spin up a little each loop, like a real motor does
        m_velocity += (m_voltage * 8.0 - m_velocity) * 0.2;
        inputs.velocityRPS = m_velocity;
        inputs.voltage = m_voltage;
    }

    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double voltage) {
        m_voltage = voltage;
    }
}

public class Intake extends SubsystemBase {
    public static enum IntakeState {
        kStow,
        kIntaking,
        kOuttaking
    }

    private final IntakeIO m_io;
    private final IntakeInputsAutoLogged m_inputs = new IntakeInputsAutoLogged();
    private final SubsystemProfiles<IntakeState> m_profiles;

    public Intake(IntakeIO io) {
        m_io = io;

        Map<IntakeState, Runnable> periodicHash = new HashMap<>();
        periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kStow, this::stowPeriodic);
        periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kIntaking, this::intakingPeriodic);
        periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kOuttaking, this::outtakingPeriodic);

        m_profiles = new SubsystemProfiles<>(periodicHash, IntakeState.kStow);
    }

    public void updateState(IntakeState state) {
        m_profiles.setCurrentProfile(state);
    }

    public IntakeState getCurrentState() {
        return m_profiles.getCurrentProfile();
    }

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        m_io.updateInputs(m_inputs);

        m_profiles.getPeriodicFunctionTimed().run();

        Logger.processInputs("Intake", m_inputs);
        Logger.recordOutput("Intake/State", m_profiles.getCurrentProfile());
    }

    public void stowPeriodic() {
        m_io.setVoltage(0.0);
    }

    public void intakingPeriodic() {
        m_io.setVoltage(8.0);
    }

    public void outtakingPeriodic() {
        m_io.setVoltage(-8.0);
    }
}

// Buttons just change the state. You'll see how this works in RobotContainer.
public class RobotContainer {
    private final Intake m_intake = new Intake(new IntakeIOSim());
    private final CommandXboxController m_driver = new CommandXboxController(0);

    public RobotContainer() {
        m_driver.a().onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kIntaking)));
        m_driver.b().onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kOuttaking)));
        m_driver.x().onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> m_intake.updateState(Intake.IntakeState.kStow)));
    }
}

Now let's build it, one layer at a time.

docs.title: Layer 1: the IO interface
docs.text:
The interface does two jobs. It lists what you can tell the hardware to do (setVoltage), and it defines everything the hardware can report, bundled into an inputs class.

IntakeIO.java
public interface IntakeIO {
    @AutoLog
    public static class IntakeInputs {
        public double velocityRPS;
        public double voltage;
    }

    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs);

    public void setVoltage(double voltage);
}

The inputs class is just a bag of public fields: speed, voltage, current, temperature, and whether the motor is even connected. The @AutoLog above it tells AdvantageKit, our logging library, to record every field in it. updateInputs fills the bag with fresh readings, and setVoltage is a command going the other way.

We control intake motors with voltage instead of a percent. A battery gives about 12 volts, so 8.0 means two thirds power, and unlike a percent, it doesn't change when the battery sags.

Your turn. IntakeIOSim is finished below, but the interface it implements doesn't exist yet. Write it.

//@ title: Write the IO interface
//@ goal: Write IntakeIO. It needs an inputs class with two double fields (velocityRPS and voltage), an updateInputs method, and a setVoltage method.
//@ lines: 24
//@ require: @AutoLog | Put @AutoLog above the inputs class.
//@ require: interface\s+IntakeIO | Declare an interface named IntakeIO.
// Write the IntakeIO interface here:


public class IntakeIOSim implements IntakeIO {
    private double m_voltage = 0.0;

    @Override
    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs) {
        inputs.velocityRPS = m_voltage * 8.0;
        inputs.voltage = m_voltage;
    }

    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double voltage) {
        m_voltage = voltage;
    }
}
//@@ harness
IntakeIO io = new IntakeIOSim();
IntakeIO.IntakeInputs inputs = new IntakeIO.IntakeInputs();
io.setVoltage(6.0);
io.updateInputs(inputs);
System.out.println(inputs.velocityRPS);
System.out.println(inputs.voltage);
//@@ expect
48.0
6.0
//@@ hint
Start with `public interface IntakeIO {`. Inside it go three things: the inputs class, and two method headers that end in a semicolon instead of a body.
//@@ hint
The inputs class is `@AutoLog public static class IntakeInputs { ... }` with `public double velocityRPS;` and `public double voltage;` inside.

Every IO class for this mechanism now has to provide exactly these two methods, and fill in exactly these two fields. That's the contract that makes real, sim and replay swappable.

Where does IntakeInputsAutoLogged come from?

You'll see the subsystem use a class called IntakeInputsAutoLogged, which you never wrote. When the robot code is built, AdvantageKit reads each @AutoLog class and generates a ...AutoLogged version of it that knows how to write every field to the log, and read it back during a replay. The editors on this page generate it for you the same way.

docs.text:
When replaying a log, the real readings come from the log file, and there is no hardware to command. So the replay class is empty: every method exists and does nothing. You wrote one of these on the previous page.

IntakeIOReplay.java
public class IntakeIOReplay implements IntakeIO {
    @Override
    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs) {}

    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double voltage) {}

docs.title: The real intake
docs.text:
This is the only class that touches a real motor. Our robot uses Kraken motors, which are controlled through a TalonFX object from the CTRE library. You don't need to memorize it, but read it, because every real IO class on our robot looks like this.

IntakeIOKraken.java (shortened)
public class IntakeIOKraken implements IntakeIO {
    private TalonFX m_motor;

    private StatusSignal<AngularVelocity> m_motorVelocity;
    private StatusSignal<Voltage> m_motorVoltage;

    private final VoltageOut m_voltageOut = new VoltageOut(0.0).withEnableFOC(true);

    public IntakeIOKraken(int port) {
        m_motor = new TalonFX(port, Ports.kDriveCanivoreName);

        // protect the motor and the battery
        var currentLimits =
            new CurrentLimitsConfigs()
                .withSupplyCurrentLimitEnable(true)
                .withSupplyCurrentLimit(CurrentLimitConstants.kIntakeRollerDefaultSupplyLimit);

        m_motor.getConfigurator().apply(new TalonFXConfiguration().withCurrentLimits(currentLimits));

        // ask the motor for the readings we want, and how often
        m_motorVelocity = m_motor.getVelocity();
        m_motorVoltage = m_motor.getMotorVoltage();
        BaseStatusSignal.setUpdateFrequencyForAll(75.0, m_motorVelocity, m_motorVoltage);
    }

    @Override
    public void updateInputs(IntakeInputs inputs) {
        BaseStatusSignal.refreshAll(m_motorVelocity, m_motorVoltage);

        inputs.velocityRPS = m_motorVelocity.getValue().in(RotationsPerSecond);
        inputs.voltage = m_motorVoltage.getValue().in(Volts);
    }

    @Override
    public void setVoltage(double voltage) {
        m_motor.setControl(m_voltageOut.withOutput(voltage));
    }
}

Compare it to the sim class. setVoltage and updateInputs are the same two methods with the same fields. The only difference is that this one gets its numbers by asking a real motor. The constructor takes the CAN id as a parameter. That's how RobotContainer, not this class, decides which motor it is.

@ title: The IO layers
? Which class is the only one that talks to a real motor?
- `Intake`
- `IntakeIO`
+ `IntakeIOKraken`
- `IntakeIOSim`
> The subsystem only knows about the `IntakeIO` interface. The Kraken class is the one place real hardware is used.

? Why is `IntakeIOReplay` empty?
- It isn't finished yet
+ During a replay the readings come from the log file and there's no hardware to command
- Replays don't use motors, so the class is deleted
- Because the Kraken class does the work
> An empty implementation is exactly right. The logged data already says what the hardware did.

? What does `updateInputs` do?
- Sends a command to the motor
+ Fills the inputs object with fresh readings
- Changes the subsystem's state
- Creates the motor
> It is the way __in__: the hardware (real or pretend) reports what it's doing.

? Why do we command a motor with voltage instead of a percent?
- Percent doesn't work on Krakens
+ The same voltage gives the same push even as the battery drains
- Voltage is easier to type
- It uses less power
> A percent of a sagging battery is a weaker push. A voltage request stays the same.

docs.title: Layer 3: the subsystem
docs.text:
Now the part where the thinking happens. The subsystem has three pieces:

  1. A list of states, as an enum. Each state is one thing the mechanism can be doing.
  2. A map from each state to the method that runs while it's in that state.
  3. A periodic() method, called every 20 ms, that ties it together.
The heart of Intake.java
public static enum IntakeState {
    kStow,
    kIntaking,
    kOuttaking
}

private SubsystemProfiles<IntakeState> m_profiles;

public Intake(IntakeIO io) {
    m_io = io;

    Map<IntakeState, Runnable> periodicHash = new HashMap<>();
    periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kStow, this::stowPeriodic);
    periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kIntaking, this::intakingPeriodic);
    periodicHash.put(IntakeState.kOuttaking, this::outtakingPeriodic);

    m_profiles = new SubsystemProfiles<>(periodicHash, IntakeState.kStow);
}

This is the interface/enum/map pattern from the previous page. SubsystemProfiles is a small helper class our team wrote that keeps track of the current state and hands back the method to run for it. It starts in kStow.

Everything else in the subsystem is small. Changing state is one line, and everything that happens in a state is a short method:

Changing state, and what each state does
public void updateState(IntakeState state) {
    m_profiles.setCurrentProfile(state);
}

public void stowPeriodic() {
    m_io.setVoltage(0.0);
}

public void intakingPeriodic() {
    m_io.setVoltage(8.0);
}

Nothing happens at the moment updateState is called. It only changes which method periodic() will run next. Here's periodic(), the method the scheduler calls every loop. The order of its lines matters.

periodic(), in order
@Override
public void periodic() {
    m_io.updateInputs(m_inputs);                       // 1. read the hardware

    m_profiles.getPeriodicFunctionTimed().run();       // 2. run the current state's method

    Logger.processInputs("Intake", m_inputs);          // 3. log what we read
    Logger.recordOutput("Intake/State", m_profiles.getCurrentProfile());  // 4. log the state
}

Read first, think second, log last. Every decision in step 2 is made with fresh readings from step 1. And because the inputs are logged, a replay can run the exact same step 2 with the exact same numbers the robot saw.

Time to add to it. This is the intake without an outtake state. Add one: a new kOuttaking state that runs the roller backwards.

docs.title: Using sensors to change state
docs.text:
Because periodic() reads the inputs before running the state, a state can look at a sensor and move the mechanism to another state by itself. This is how we stop an intake the moment it has a game piece.

A state that changes itself
public void intakingPeriodic() {
    m_io.setVoltage(IntakeConstants.kIntakeVoltage);

    // current spikes when the rollers squeeze a game piece
    if (m_inputs.current > IntakeConstants.kHasPieceCurrent) {
        updateState(IntakeState.kHold);
    }
}

The operator pressed intake once. The subsystem decided for itself when it was done. Our real intake does exactly this, along with checking whether its pivot has reached an angle before spinning the rollers.

@ title: Subsystem states
? Why is the first line of `periodic()` a call to `updateInputs`?
- It's required by Java
+ So the state's method decides using fresh readings
- So the log file is smaller
- To reset the motor
> Read first, think second, log last.

? You call `intake.updateState(IntakeState.kIntaking)`. When do the rollers start spinning?
- Instantly, inside `updateState`
+ On the next `periodic()`, when the new state's method runs
- Never, you need a command for that
- When the driver presses A again
> `updateState` only changes which method runs next. `periodic()` does the work.

? You add a new state `kHold` to the enum but forget to register a method for it in the map. What happens when the subsystem enters `kHold`?
- The rollers stop safely
+ It prints a warning (and does nothing), because there's no method to run for that state
- It fixes itself
- The robot code won't compile
> `SubsystemProfiles` warns you in the console when a state has no method. Each state in the enum needs a line in the map.

? What decides whether a subsystem is connected to real or simulated hardware?
- `Intake`
+ `RobotContainer`, which hands the subsystem an IO class when it builds it
- `periodic()`
- `stowPeriodic()`
> The subsystem only talks to the interface, so it never knows which IO class it got. Choosing real or sim is one decision, made in one place. (There are small exceptions, like picking simulation-friendly PID numbers. You'll see one on the Constants page.)

docs.title: What about commands?
docs.text:
If you've followed an FRC tutorial, you may have seen subsystems that build commands for each action. That's a perfectly good style, and it's what the WPILib documentation teaches. Here is what the two approaches look like for the same button.

Commands in the subsystemStates (our team) 
// in IntakeSubsystem
public Command intake() {
    return startEnd(() -> m_motor.set(0.8), () -> m_motor.set(0.0));
}

// in RobotContainer
m_driver.a().whileTrue(m_intake.intake());

// in Intake
public void updateState(IntakeState state) {
    m_profiles.setCurrentProfile(state);
}

// in RobotContainer (or RobotState), when the driver presses A
m_intake.updateState(IntakeState.kIntaking);

We use states because a real robot rarely has one mechanism doing one thing. Picking up a game piece means the intake, the indexer and the elevator all have to change at the same moment, and then react to sensors. With states, one place (RobotState, which you'll see soon) can set all of them, and the log shows each subsystem's state at every moment. We still use commands where they fit best: driving and autonomous routines.

docs.title: On a real robot
docs.text:
Real files begin with a package line and imports, which this page left out. They also use your team's constants. A few details:

  • IntakeInputsAutoLogged is generated when the code is built. You'll see it used but never find a file for it.
  • Alerts: our subsystems turn on a dashboard alert when a motor reports it's disconnected, so a loose wire shows up before a match, not during it.
  • Timing: each subsystem logs how long its periodic() took, so we notice if one gets slow.
  • Tuning: numbers like voltages are not plain doubles in our constants. They're tunable from the dashboard while the robot runs. See Constants.

docs.title: Setting up for code
docs.text: Before you start coding, its always best to set up an environment where you can keep track of your code. Create a folder where you can store your code. Personally, I have a Java folder in my Documents.

docs.title: Methods and Members
docs.text: Objects in Java are made up of two main parts: members and methods. Members hold information about the object, while methods are the actions the object can do.

docs.title: Members
docs.text:
Members, also called attributes or variables, are characteristics of an object that you can define and change later. For example, if you were making a car, you might want to define its color, top speed, and miles per gallon. Keep in mind that these values are allowed to change, so something like fuel level, which changes over time, would still be a member.

When defining a member in Java, you must follow proper syntax. The correct way to define a member is shown below.

Syntax

Syntax is a set of rules you must follow for Java to be able to understand you. Much like how English requires proper grammar, Java requires proper syntax to work. In Java, most statements (like variable definitions or method calls) must end with a semicolon (;).

Syntax for defining a member
type   name    = value;

int wheelCount = 4;

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
Whenever you create a member, you must first assign it a type. Type is a reference to the data type of the variable. The following are data types used in FRC Java: int, String, double, and boolean.

  • int: This stands for integer. An integer is any whole number that we would want to use. For the car example, we might use int for the number of wheels, since we can't have a fraction of a wheel.
  • String: A string is any combination of characters. This is used almost exclusively for logging errors in FRC Java. If we didn't know why the car wasn't driving, we might want to print out "not driving" at times to test it, which would use a String.
  • double: This is used for decimal values. For the car example, we might use double for the car’s speed, since a car can travel at 55.5 miles per hour or 32.7 km/h, not just whole numbers.
  • boolean: This data type can only be either true or false (lowercase only). It is used in conditionals, which is ued to make decisions in code. For example, we might say, "if the car in on, start moving." The "if the car is on" part could be represented by a boolean.

docs.title: Name
docs.text:
The name of a member can be anything you like. Although this is the case, it is best give a member a name that is representative of what it is. For example, fuelLevel would be a much better name for the car's fuel level than thing1. Names must be one word to follow proper syntax, otherwise Java would throw an error.

Camel Case

Did you notice that the capitalization was funky in the code above? This is called camel case, which is when we capitalize the first letter of every word in a variable, save for the first word. For example, "constant speed" would be written as constantSpeed.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: The value of the member must match the type it is assigned. For example, you cannot assign a value of true to an int object, as int expects a whole number. As long as it falls within the expected type, the value can be as large as you need it to be.

docs.title: Using members
docs.text:
The value of members can be used and updated throughout your code, which is what makes them so powerful. Once you've defined the type for the member, you can update it without having to redefine its type. In the below example, message is created as a String, and its value gets changed.

//@ title: Change a member
//@ goal: Press Run. Then change the second message to anything you like and run it again.
String message = "hello world";
System.out.println(message);
message = "Java is cool";
System.out.println(message);
What does System.out.println do?

It prints whatever you give it to the console, then moves to a new line. That's how you "see" what your code is doing, and it's the first debugging tool you'll reach for in FRC too, where the output appears in the Driver Station console.

docs.title: Try all four types
docs.text:
Here is one of each type. Press Run, then break it on purpose: change 4 to 4.5, or put "four" where the 4 is. Reading Java's error messages is a skill, and the best way to learn it is to cause some.

//@ title: The four types
//@ goal: Run it, then try to break it. What does Java say when you put a decimal in an int?
int wheelCount = 4;
double speed = 55.5;
String name = "Acura";
boolean isOn = true;

System.out.println(name + " has " + wheelCount + " wheels");
System.out.println("Speed: " + speed);
System.out.println("Running: " + isOn);

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Methods, also known as functions, are actions that an object can do. In the case of the car example, methods could be drive(), turnOnLights(), and slowDown().

The proper syntax to define a method is shown below:

Syntax for defining a method
accessModifier returnType name(parameters) {
    // code goes here
}

public void slowDown() {
    // code goes here
}

docs.title: Access modifier
docs.text: The first part of defining a method is the access modifier. This tells Java who can access, or run, the method. There are three types of access modifiers: public, private, and protected. Public means that anyone can access it from anywhere, including from outside the file the method is created in. Private means that access is limited to a certain level, such as only the current class. Protected, which isn't used as much in FRC, is more accessible than Private, but is still limited in access, typically only to the current class and its subclasses.

docs.title: Return type
docs.text:
The second part of a method is its return type. The return type tells Java if you plan to return, or output, some value to whoever called the function. This is done using the return statement. For example, when you speed up the car, you don't get any information back, thus it wouldn't require a return statement. However, checking the navigation would require back some map data for you to be able to tell where you are, which would require a return statement.

Example use of return
public int calculateRemainingMiles() {
    int milesRemaining = "insert cool math here";
    return milesRemaining;
}

In the above example, you can see how the number of miles remaining is being returned to whoever called the method. In this case, since milesRemaining is an int, the return type is set to int.

Here is a method you can run. It takes in a number and gives one back. Notice that the method does nothing until something calls it.

//@ title: A method that returns a value
//@ goal: Run it. Then change the numbers in the two calls at the bottom.
public int milesRemaining(int tankSize, int milesPerGallon) {
    return tankSize * milesPerGallon;
}

System.out.println(milesRemaining(10, 25));
System.out.println(milesRemaining(15, 30));

docs.title: Name
docs.text: Much like members, the name of a method can be anything you want. It is common practice to name it something related to what the method does.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameters are things that the method can take in to manipulate or make decisions. Not all methods need parameters. The following example shows a parameter vehicleType being used to determine how many wheels a car has.

//@ title: A method with a parameter
//@ goal: Run it, then call the method with "truck" instead of "sedan".
public void determineVehicleWheels(String vehicleType) {
    if (vehicleType.equals("sedan")) {
        System.out.println("This has 4 wheels");
    }
    else if (vehicleType.equals("truck")) {
        System.out.println("This has 8 wheels");
    }
}

determineVehicleWheels("sedan");

Compare Strings with .equals

To check whether two Strings hold the same text, use .equals("text"), not ==. The == operator asks whether two Strings are the very same object in memory, which can give you a wrong answer even when the words match. You'll see .equals used from here on.

docs.title: Curly brackets/braces
docs.text: The {} is the final key component of a method. This is what will serve as the boundary or fence of the code for your method. The code you write for your method to do something must lie withint the opening, {, and closing ,}, brackets.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text: Time to write some code of your own. Each challenge checks your work when you press Check my code. If you get stuck, the hints reveal one at a time.

docs.title: Members or methods?
docs.text:
Each of these is part of code that creates an animal. Decide whether it is a member or a method.

@ title: Members or methods?
? `int numLegs;`
- Member
- Method
+ Member
> It holds information about the animal, and has no parentheses or body.

? `public void eat() {}`
+ Method
- Member
> The parentheses and `{}` body make it an action the animal can do.

? `private int returnFriendCount() {}`
+ Method
- Member
> `private` is its access modifier and `int` is its return type, but the parentheses and body show it's a method.

? `String name;`
+ Member
- Method
> A `String` holds text, which is information about the animal.

? `double hoursOld;`
+ Member
- Method
> It stores a decimal number describing the animal.
