docs.title: Lesson 2: Comparision Operators, Conditionals And For Loops
Comparision operators
docs.text:
Operators in Java are typically grouped into categories depending on their function. One of these is the comparision operators, which are used to compare two values. This is especially important for conditionals and for loops, as it defines when they run or how long to run for. Below is a list of operators which are used commonly.

  • ==: Equal to (5 == 5 → true)

  • !=: Not equal to (5 != 3 → true)

  • >: Greater than (7 > 4 → true)

  • <: Less than (2 < 6 → true)

  • >=: Greater than or equal to (7 >= 7 → true)

  • <=: Less than or equal to (3 <= 5 → true)

Comparision operators will output a boolean value, either true or false, depending on the values provided. You can use the output for setting members, using conditionals, and more. Below is an example of using comparision operators.

//@ title: Comparison operators
//@ goal: Run it, then change the numbers and see which lines print true or false.
boolean isGreater = 5 > 7;
System.out.println("5 > 7 is " + isGreater);
System.out.println("5 == 5 is " + (5 == 5));
System.out.println("7 != 3 is " + (7 != 3));
System.out.println("3 <= 3 is " + (3 <= 3));

if (5 == 5) {
    System.out.println("This is true");
}

== vs =

A single = assigns a value (int x = 5;). A double == compares two values (x == 5). Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

docs.title: Arithmetic operators
docs.text:
Arithmetic operators are used for basic mathematical operations, such as adding or subtracting two values. Here is a list of common arithmetic operators:

  • +: Addition
  • -: Subtraction
  • *: Multiplication
  • /: Division
  • %: Modulus (remainder after division)

Using arithmetic operators is simple. Just place them between the two values you want to use it on.

Before you run this, work out what it prints. Type your prediction in the box, then press Check my prediction.

//@ title: Predict the output
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: What will these two lines print? Put each answer on its own line.
int a = 5;
int b = 6;
System.out.println(a + b);
System.out.println(a % b);
//@@ explain
`5 + 6` is 11. For `5 % 6`, 6 doesn't fit into 5 at all, so the whole 5 is left over as the remainder.

docs.title: Integer division
docs.text:
When you divide two ints, Java throws away the decimal part. This catches out almost everyone at least once, and it matters in FRC code, where you'll often divide to turn encoder counts into distances.

//@ title: Integer division
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: Predict all three lines. Careful with the first two!
System.out.println(7 / 2);
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);
System.out.println(1 / 2);
//@@ explain
Two `int`s divide as an `int`, so `7 / 2` is 3 and `1 / 2` is 0. If either side is a `double`, you get a decimal answer: `7 / 2.0` is 3.5.

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
A conditional is a way to make choices based on the current situation. The program asks itself is this true?, and if so do this, otherwise, do something else. The diagram below shows a visual representation of a conditional.

graph LR
    A[Is this true?] --> |Yes|B[Do This];
    A[Is this true?] --> |No|C[Do This Instead];

Java has three types of conditional statements, if, else if, and else.

docs.title: If statements
docs.text:
An if statement is the first part of any conditional. It initiates the check by asking if something is equal to some value. The syntax for an if statement is shown below.

if (condition) {
    // do this
}

Run it below. Then change color to "blue" and run it again. Nothing prints, because the condition is false and there is no else.

//@ title: Your first if statement
//@ goal: Change color to "blue". What happens?
String color = "red";

if (color.equals("red")) {
    System.out.println("The car is red");
}

The condition can be anything that you want Java to evaluate. It could be some basic math operations, such as 5>6, which would evaluate to false. It could also use variables (members) from last lesson, such as if(boolean), which will always evaluate to either true or false, since those are the only two values a boolean can store. The above example checks if the color of the vehicle is red, and if so, print out "The car is red".

docs.title: Else statements
docs.text:
An else statement is the next conditional in the flow of a conditional chain. This serves as the alternative action if the first if statement evaluates to false.

if (condition) {
    // do this
}

else {
    // do this
}

//@ title: if and else
//@ goal: Run it with each color: "red", then something else.
String color = "green";

if (color.equals("red")) {
    System.out.println("The car is red");
}
else {
    System.out.println("The car is not red");
}

In the example above, the first if statement checks whether the car is red. If the car is not red, that condition evaluates to false, and the program moves to the else block. The else block doesn’t have its own condition, it simply runs whenever the if statement fails, acting like a “catch-all” for everything that wasn’t true.

docs.title: Else if statements
docs.text:
What if you wanted to check if the car was blue? Although you could technically put multiple if statements one-after-another, Java has an efficient way to check different conditions, called an else if block. Check out the example below to see the difference.

Bad exampleGood example 
if (vehicle.color.equals("red")) {
    System.out.println("The car is red");
}

if (vehicle.color.equals("blue")) {
    System.out.println("The car is blue");
}

if (vehicle.color.equals("orange")) {
    System.out.println("The car is orange");
}

else {
    System.out.println("The car is not red");
}

if (vehicle.color.equals("red")) {
    System.out.println("The car is red");
}

else if (vehicle.color.equals("blue")) {
    System.out.println("The car is blue");
}

else if (vehicle.color.equals("orange")) {
    System.out.println("The car is orange");
}

else {
    System.out.println("The car is not red");
}

Notice how only the middle two if statements were changed to else if. This small change makes the code much more efficient:

  • With else if, Java stops checking as soon as one condition is true. For example, if the car is blue, Java checks red, then checks blue, and then exits the chain immediately.

  • With separate if statements, Java would still check all the other conditions, even if one was already true. That means if the car is blue, it would still check orange, which is unnecessary.

By using else if, you make your code both faster and easier to read.

//@ title: An else if chain
//@ goal: Try "red", "blue", "orange" and "purple". Which branch runs for each?
String color = "blue";

if (color.equals("red")) {
    System.out.println("The car is red");
}
else if (color.equals("blue")) {
    System.out.println("The car is blue");
}
else if (color.equals("orange")) {
    System.out.println("The car is orange");
}
else {
    System.out.println("The car is some other color");
}

docs.title: Conditionals with booleans
docs.text:
Conditionals can also be used with booleans directly, since they can only be either true or false. The snippet below provides an example.

//@ title: Conditionals with booleans
//@ goal: Run it, then set carIsOn to false.
boolean carIsOn = true;

if (carIsOn) {
    System.out.println("Ready to drive");
}
else {
    System.out.println("Turn car on to drive");
}
You wouldn't need to say if (carIsOn==true), since Java knows that since its a boolean value, it can only be true or false, so it handles the checking for you.

Usage of else and else if

You won't always need an else if or even an else condition. This depends on your code and if you want to do something if the first if condition is false.

docs.title: For Loops
docs.text: A for loop is a way to repeat a block of code a set number of times. Think of it like this: imagine you’re told to do 10 push-ups. Instead of someone saying “Do a push-up, do a push-up, do a push-up…” ten times, they just say “Do 10 push-ups.” A for loop works the same way — it repeats your instructions automatically until the count is done.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The proper way to write a for loop uses a variable, typically called i, to keep track of how many times the loop has run. An example is shown below.

//@ title: Do 10 push-ups
//@ goal: Run it. Then change the 10 to a different number, and try starting i at 1 instead of 0.
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    System.out.println("Push-up number " + (i + 1));
}

You can break down the inside, int i=0;i<10;i++, into three main parts: Initialization, condition, and update/increment.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text: Just like when you create a member, Java needs a variable inside the loop to keep track of how many times it has run. This follows the same pattern you’ve already seen: type name = value. In the example above, the type is int, the name is i, and the starting value is 0. That means the counter variable i begins at 0, and Java will use it to control how many times the loop repeats. You may also begin the counter i above 0, which is typically used when counting down.

docs.title: Condition
docs.text:
This part of the for loop statement — the condition — controls how many times your code will repeat. The condition is checked before each iteration, and the loop only continues if it evaluates to true. The condition is usually written in the form: name<value. Here, name is the variable from the initialization, and value sets the stopping point.

Use of <

At first glance, a condition like i < 10 might seem like the loop will only run 9 times. However, since the counter i starts at 0, the loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, ..., 9, which is 10 iterations total. This “zero-based counting” is standard practice in Java (and most programming languages).

Examples of conditions you can use:

  • Less than (i < 10) → loop runs while i is less than 10.

  • Less than or equal to (i <= 10) → loop runs while i is less than or equal to 10 (so it runs 11 times if starting from 0).

  • Greater than (i > 0) → often used when counting down.

  • Greater than or equal to (i >= 0) → loop continues until i drops below 0.

  • Equality check (i == 5) → less common, but possible if you only want to run when i hits a specific value.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
The update (also called the increment) is the last portion of a for loop. It controls how the loop variable changes after each iteration. In most cases, such as the example, this is written as i++, which means “increase i by 1.”

The update is essential — without it, the condition might never be met, causing an infinite loop.

Examples of updates:

  • i++: increases by 1 (most common).

  • i--: decreases by 1 (useful for counting down).

  • i += 2: increases by 2 (counts even numbers if starting at 0).

  • i *= 2: doubles the value each time.

The update doesn’t always have to be an increment; it can be any expression that changes the loop variable. This flexibility allows for loops to handle many patterns, like skipping numbers, looping backward, or growing exponentially.

docs.title: Combining initialization, condition, and update
docs.text:
The example below shows how you can use the three components of a for loop to count down from 10, skipping every other number.

//@ title: Counting down by twos
//@ goal: Run it. Then make it count down by threes, or count up from 0 to 20 by fives.
for (int i = 10; i >= 0; i -= 2) {
    System.out.print(i + " ");
}

Here, the i variable starts at 10 and we decrease it by 2 every time the loop runs. This continues while i is greater than or equal to 0.

docs.title: Predict the output
docs.text:
Look at the code below. What will it print? Work it out on paper first, one value of i at a time, then type your answer and press Check my prediction.

//@ title: Even, odd, or big?
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: Type exactly what this prints, one line per line of output.
for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) {
        System.out.println(i + " is even");
    } else if (i > 3) {
        System.out.println(i + " is greater than 3 and odd");
    } else {
        System.out.println(i + " is odd");
    }
}
//@@ explain
Even numbers hit the first branch. For the odd ones, only 5 is greater than 3, so it gets the second branch.

docs.title: Challenge 1: Limit a motor speed
docs.text:
Motors in FRC accept a speed from -1.0 to 1.0. Anything beyond that is invalid, so robot code often clamps a value into the allowed range. You can do that with the conditionals you just learned.

//@ title: Clamp a speed
//@ goal: Finish the method so it returns 1.0 if speed is above 1.0, returns -1.0 if speed is below -1.0, and otherwise returns speed unchanged.
//@ require: if | Use an if statement.
public double clamp(double speed) {
    // your code here
    return speed;
}
//@@ harness
System.out.println(clamp(0.5));
System.out.println(clamp(2.3));
System.out.println(clamp(-5.0));
System.out.println(clamp(-0.25));
//@@ expect
0.5
1.0
-1.0
-0.25
//@@ hint
You need two checks: one for speed too high, and one for speed too low.
//@@ hint
`if (speed > 1.0) { return 1.0; }` stops the method right there and sends back 1.0. Write the matching check for the low end.
//@@ solution
public double clamp(double speed) {
    if (speed > 1.0) {
        return 1.0;
    } else if (speed < -1.0) {
        return -1.0;
    }
    return speed;
}
//@@ explain
This exact idea is in WPILib as `MathUtil.clamp`. You'll meet it again when you start driving motors.

docs.title: Challenge 2: Count down
docs.text:
//@ title: Liftoff
//@ goal: Use a for loop to print 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 on separate lines, then print Liftoff!
//@ require: for\s*\( | Use a for loop.
// Write your loop here:

//@@ expect
5
4
3
2
1
Liftoff!
//@@ hint
Start i at 5, keep going while i is at least 1, and use i-- to count down.
//@@ solution
for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--) {
    System.out.println(i);
}
System.out.println("Liftoff!");
//@@ explain
Counting down just means starting high, checking with `>=`, and decreasing with `i--`.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
A class in Java is like a blueprint for something you are trying to make. Imagine a blueprint for the car from the last lesson. You cannot physically drive the blueprint, but you can follow it to make the actual car. Similarly, classes themselves cannot do anything, but the class can be used to create an object that can do things.

All methods and members reside in a class. Most Java projects start with a Main class, titled Main.java. This is where your main code lives. For FRC, Main.java is taken care of by WPILib, so we won't ever have to touch it.

Important

Your class name MUST match the name and capitalization of the file for it to run. It is something that is specific to Java and will cause an error if not followed.

Car.java
public class Car {
   // Your methods and members will go here
}

Writing classes in Java is pretty simple. All it requires is the name of the class. The above example creates a class named Car in the Car.java file.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
An object is a real, usable thing created from a class, which is like its blueprint or recipe. The class describes what the object can have and can do, but by itself, it’s not something you can use yet.

When you create an object, it gets its own data (called members or fields), which stores information about that specific object. It also gets methods, which are the actions it can perform.

For example, for the Car class: it might say that every car has a color, speed, and fuelLevel, and that it can drive(), brake(), or honk(). When you make a car object, you now have a real car in your program: it might be red, going 50 mph, and able to honk whenever you call myCar.honk().

docs.title: How to create an object
docs.text:
Creating an object, or making it exist, is called instantiation. Instantiation refers to the fact that you are creating a unique instance of a class. Although many cars may use the same blueprint to build them, they may vary in tiny details, such as their color, top speed, or model. Each specific car is called an instance. The snippet below shows how to instantiate an object.

class name = new class();
Car Acura = new Car("red", 50);
To instantiate and object, you must first specify its class. Just like how you must tell Java what type of member you are creating, you must tell it what type of object you are creating.

Then, you provide a name for the object. Much like methods and members, the name of an object is anything that describes what the object is.

Next, you must use the new operator to create a new car.

Finally, you must specify the class once again so that Java knows what blueprint to use to build the object.

Additionally, if your class contains members, you can define it inside the parenthesis. This takes advantage of the object being a unique instance, meaning you can have multiple Acuras of a variety of colors. In this example, the car is red and starts at 50 mph.

docs.title: Using an object
docs.text:
Java is an object-oriented program language, which means that objects will take the members and methods of a class. This allows objects created by instantiation to perform actions of its assigned class. This is done using the dot operator, which is simply a . placed after the object name, which allows you to access the methods and members of the instance.

//@ title: Two cars from one blueprint
//@ goal: Run it. Then add a third car of your own, give it a color, and make it drive.
//@ lines: 22
public class Car {
    public String color;

    public Car(String color) {
        this.color = color;
    }

    public void drive() {
        System.out.println("The " + color + " car is driving");
    }
}

Car acura = new Car("red");
acura.drive();
System.out.println(acura.color);

Car toyota = new Car("orange");
toyota.drive();
System.out.println(toyota.color);

In the above example, we have instantiated two unique cars, an Acura and a Toyota. Since both the Acura and the Toyota are made from the Car class, they can both drive and stop. However, since they are objects unique of each other, they each have their own color, which is also accessed using the dot operator.

docs.title: Constructors
docs.text:
A constructor is a special method in Java that connects your object instantiation to the class blueprint. Think of it like this: The object instiation is a person looking to get a house built, the class is the blueprint for the house, and the constructor is the one who builds the house using the blueprint and adding in the buyer's preferences.

In the above example, the constructor would be in charge of making a red car that starts at 50 mph using a blueprint for a generic car.

graph LR
    A[Object Instantiation] -->|I want a red car| B[Constructor];
    D[Class] --> |Here's instructions for a car of color _x_|B;
    B --> C[Red Car Created];

docs.title: Writing a constructor
docs.text:
Constructors exist in the class. Highlighted below is an example constructor for the Car class.

Car.java

public class Car {
    private String color;

    public Car(String color) {
        this.color = color;
    }
}
This constructor assigns the color specified during instantiation to the specific instance of the car.

The word this means "the object being built right now". It separates the object's own color field (this.color) from the parameter that is also called color. Try the example below, and add a second parameter to the constructor.

//@ title: Add a field to the constructor
//@ goal: Run it. Then add a topSpeed field (an int), take it as a second constructor parameter, and print it too. Remember to change the call at the bottom.
//@ lines: 16
public class Car {
    private String color;

    public Car(String color) {
        this.color = color;
    }

    public void printInfo() {
        System.out.println("A " + color + " car");
    }
}

Car acura = new Car("red");
acura.printInfo();

docs.title: Combining Classes, Objects, and Constructors
Identify the parts
docs.text:
//@ title: Read the code
//@ mode: predict
//@ goal: What does this program print? (Hint: follow the constructor.)
public class Car {
    private String color;

    public Car(String color) {
        this.color = color;
    }

    public void honk() {
        System.out.println(color + " car says Beep!");
    }
}

Car acura = new Car("red");
acura.honk();
//@@ explain
`new Car("red")` runs the constructor, which stores `"red"` in this car's `color`. Then `honk()` uses that stored color.

Now match each piece of that code to its name.

@ title: Class, object, or constructor?
? Which part is the **class**?
| public class Car { ... }
| public Car(String color) { ... }
| Car acura = new Car("red");
+ `public class Car { ... }`
- `public Car(String color) { ... }`
- `Car acura = new Car("red");`
> The class is the blueprint. It's the whole `Car` definition.

? Which part is the **constructor**?
| public class Car { ... }
| public Car(String color) { ... }
| Car acura = new Car("red");
- `public class Car { ... }`
+ `public Car(String color) { ... }`
- `Car acura = new Car("red");`
> A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type.

? Which part **instantiates an object**?
| public class Car { ... }
| public Car(String color) { ... }
| Car acura = new Car("red");
- `public class Car { ... }`
- `public Car(String color) { ... }`
+ `Car acura = new Car("red");`
> The `new` keyword builds a real Car from the blueprint, and `acura` is that object.

? How many objects exist after these two lines run? `Car a = new Car("red");` and `Car b = new Car("red");`
- 1, because they are both red
+ 2
- 0, because nothing was printed
> Every use of `new` creates a separate object, even when the contents are identical.

docs.title: Challenge 1: Write a constructor
docs.text:
An FRC robot cares a lot about battery voltage. Finish this class by writing its constructor.

//@ title: Battery constructor
//@ goal: Write a constructor for Battery that takes a double called voltage and stores it in the voltage field.
//@ lines: 12
//@ require: public\s+Battery\s*\( | The constructor must be named Battery and be public.
//@ require: this\.voltage | Use this.voltage to set the field.
public class Battery {
    private double voltage;

    // Write the constructor here

    public double getVoltage() {
        return voltage;
    }

    public boolean isLow() {
        return voltage < 11.5;
    }
}
//@@ harness
Battery full = new Battery(12.6);
Battery weak = new Battery(10.9);
System.out.println(full.getVoltage());
System.out.println(full.isLow());
System.out.println(weak.getVoltage());
System.out.println(weak.isLow());
//@@ expect
12.6
false
10.9
true
//@@ hint
A constructor looks like a method with no return type, named exactly like the class.
//@@ hint
`public Battery(double voltage) { ... }`. Inside the braces, assign the parameter to the field.
//@@ solution
public class Battery {
    private double voltage;

    public Battery(double voltage) {
        this.voltage = voltage;
    }

    public double getVoltage() {
        return voltage;
    }

    public boolean isLow() {
        return voltage < 11.5;
    }
}
//@@ explain
Each Battery object remembers its own voltage, so the full battery and the weak battery behave differently from the same class.

public class Car {

    public int speed;

    }

    public void describe() {

}

// Create your cars below:

//@@ expect
A red car going 50 mph
A blue car going 70 mph
//@@ hint
`Car name = new Car("red", 50);` creates one. Give each car its own variable name.
//@@ hint
Use the dot operator to call a method: `name.describe();`
//@@ solution
public class Car {
    public String color;
    public int speed;

    public Car(String color, int speed) {
        this.color = color;
        this.speed = speed;
    }

    public void describe() {

docs.text:
@ title: Lesson 1 quiz
? Which data type would you use to store the number of wheels on a car?
- double
- String
+ int
- boolean
> A wheel count is a whole number, so `int` fits. `double` is for decimals.

? Which line correctly creates a member?
- `int wheelCount == 4;`
- `wheelCount int = 4;`
+ `int wheelCount = 4;`
- `int wheel count = 4;`
> The pattern is `type name = value;`. Names can't contain spaces, and `==` compares rather than assigns.

? What is wrong with this line?
| int speed = 55.5;
- Nothing, it is fine
+ A decimal can't be stored in an `int`
- `speed` is a reserved word
- It is missing the word `public`
> `55.5` has a decimal part, so the type should be `double`. Java reports this as a "lossy conversion".

? Which of these are valid camelCase names? (Pick all that apply.)
+ fuelLevel
+ topSpeed
- FuelLevel
- top_speed
- top speed
> Camel case starts lowercase and capitalizes each new word with no spaces or underscores.

? In `public int calculateMiles() { ... }`, what is `int`?
- The access modifier
+ The return type
- The name
- A parameter
> `public` is the access modifier, `int` is the return type, and `calculateMiles` is the name.

? What does `void` mean as a return type?
- The method returns zero
+ The method does not return anything
- The method can't be called
- The method is private
> Use `void` when a method just does something and doesn't send a value back.

? Which statement about `private` is true?
- Anyone can call the method from anywhere
+ Access is limited, for example to the current class
- It can only be used on members
- It makes the method run faster
> `public` opens something up to everyone. `private` restricts it.

docs.title: Lesson 2: Operators, conditionals and loops
docs.text:
@ title: Lesson 2 quiz
? What does `10 % 3` evaluate to?
- 3
- 0
+ 1
- 3.33
> `%` gives the remainder. 3 goes into 10 three times with 1 left over.

? What does this print?
| System.out.println(9 / 2);
- 4.5
+ 4
- 5
- 4.0
> Dividing two `int`s drops the decimal part.

? What does this print?
| System.out.println(9 / 2.0);
+ 4.5
- 4
- 5
- 4.0
> One side is a `double`, so the answer keeps its decimal.

? Which operator __compares__ two values for equality?
- `=`
+ `==`
- `!=`
- `=>`
> A single `=` assigns, and a double `==` compares.

? What does this print?
| int x = 7;
| if (x > 5) {
|     System.out.println("big");
| } else if (x > 3) {
|     System.out.println("medium");
| } else {
|     System.out.println("small");
| }
+ big
- medium
- small
- big and medium
> Java stops at the first true branch. `7 > 5` is true, so `else if` is never checked.

? How many times does this loop run?
| for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { }
- 9
+ 10
- 11
- Forever
> `i` takes the values 0 through 9, which is 10 times.

? What does this print?
| for (int i = 10; i >= 0; i -= 5) {
|     System.out.print(i + " ");
| }
- 10 5
+ 10 5 0
- 10 5 0 -5
- 0 5 10
> It starts at 10 and subtracts 5 each time, stopping once `i >= 0` is false.

? Which is the best way to check whether a `String` named `color` holds "red"?
- `color = "red"`
- `color == "red"`
+ `color.equals("red")`
- `if color is "red"`
> `.equals` compares the text itself. `==` can give a wrong answer for Strings.

? Which of these will cause an infinite loop?
- `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }`
+ `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i--) { }`
- `for (int i = 3; i > 0; i--) { }`
> In the middle one `i` keeps getting smaller, so `i < 3` is always true.

docs.title: Lesson 3: Classes, objects and constructors
docs.text:
@ title: Lesson 3 quiz
? What is the relationship between a class and an object?
- They are the same thing
+ A class is the blueprint, an object is a real thing built from it
- An object is the blueprint, a class is a real thing built from it
- Objects can only be made without a class
> Many objects, each with its own data, can be built from one class.

? The file contains `public class Car { }`. What must the file be named?
- car.java
- MyCar.java
+ Car.java
- Main.java
> A public class's name must match the file name exactly, including capitalization.

? What does the `new` keyword do?
- Declares a new variable type
+ Creates a new object from a class
- Defines a new method
- Imports a class
> `new Car("red")` builds a fresh `Car` object and calls its constructor.

? What is special about a constructor? (Pick all that apply.)
+ It has the same name as the class
+ It has no return type
+ It runs when you use `new`
- It must be `void`
- It can only be called once per program
> A constructor looks like a method without a return type, and `new` calls it each time you make an object.

? In this constructor, what does `this.color` refer to?
| public Car(String color) {
|     this.color = color;
| }
- The parameter named `color`
+ The `color` field of the object being built
- A different class
- The color of the computer screen
> `this` points at the object itself, so `this.color` is the field and plain `color` is the parameter.

? What does this print?
| Car a = new Car("red");
| Car b = new Car("blue");
| System.out.println(a.color);
+ red
- blue
- red blue
- Nothing, it's an error
> Each object keeps its own copy of the fields. `a` was built with "red".

? Which line makes the car drive, assuming `acura` is a `Car`?
- `acura->drive();`
- `drive(acura);`
+ `acura.drive();`
- `Car.acura.drive;`
> The dot operator accesses an object's methods and members.

docs.title: Why Java?
docs.text:
Java is a versatile programming language that is used for various sorts of applications, ranging from entriprise and mobile applications, IOT projects, and, in our case, for FRC programming. Java is one of the three officially supported programming lanuages for FRC: Java, Python, and C++.

Many FRC teams choose Java for its ease-of-use compared to C++ and its versatility when compared to Python. Below is an example of the same code, using a joystick to control a motor, written in Java, C++, and Python.

JavaC++Python 
// Import WPILib classes
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.Joystick;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.PWMVictorSPX;

public class Robot extends TimedRobot {
    private final Joystick joystick = new Joystick(0);
    private final PWMVictorSPX motor = new PWMVictorSPX(0);

    @Override
    public void teleopPeriodic() {
        double speed = joystick.getY();   // Strongly typed: always a double
        motor.set(speed);                 // Easy, safe, no pointers
    }
}

#include <frc/Joystick.h>
#include <frc/PWMVictorSPX.h>
#include <frc/TimedRobot.h>

class Robot : public frc::TimedRobot {
    frc::Joystick joystick{0};
    frc::PWMVictorSPX motor{0};

    void TeleopPeriodic() override {
        double speed = joystick.GetY();  // Works, but watch for precision issues
        motor.Set(speed);                // Must manage lifetimes carefully
    }
};

from wpilib import Joystick, PWMVictorSPX, TimedRobot

class MyRobot(TimedRobot):
    def robotInit(self):
        self.joystick = Joystick(0)
        self.motor = PWMVictorSPX(0)

    def teleopPeriodic(self):
        speed = self.joystick.getY()  # Dynamically typed
        self.motor.set(speed)

In the example above, you can see that Java’s syntax is easier to read and understand compared to C++. For instance, creating objects in Java uses the simple new keyword, while C++ requires :: and more complex type declarations, which can be confusing for beginners.

Python may look simpler than Java at first glance, but it isn’t fully supported by WPILib. This means that when you try more advanced robot programming tasks, Python can quickly become limiting.

Note

This course will not cover the entire Java language, as it is vast and continually expanding. However, it will introduce you to the basics you need to write effective FRC robot code, allowing you to confidently control motors, read sensors, and structure your robot programs for both teleoperated and autonomous modes.

In summary, Java strikes a balance between readability, safety, and official FRC support. It allows new programmers to quickly understand and write robot code without getting bogged down by complex syntax or unsupported libraries. With this foundation, you’re now ready to dive into your first Java robot project and start controlling motors and sensors on your robot.
